This initial generation of the mind possesses five virtuous characteristics: First, the correct aspiration (*samyak-praṇidhāna*) inherent in this initial generation of the mind universally encompasses all other correct aspirations; therefore, the generation of the mind has this initial correct aspiration as its essential nature (*svabhāva*). Second, it refers to the arising of the vow:

"May I certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and may I bring about the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, ultimately establishing them in final *nirvāṇa* and within the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the generation of the mind has this resolute seeking as its mode of activity (*ākāra*).
Third, because it takes great enlightenment and sentient beings as its object, it possesses an objective referent (*ālambana*).

Fourth, because this initial production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*) encompasses all sublime practices and can counteract all the evil deeds of sentient beings, it is associated with all meritorious qualities.
Fifth, this initial right aspiration is the most supreme and foremost among all mundane and supramundane aspirations.

This initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is called "entering into unsurpassed awakening" (*anuttara-bodhi*); within the first eon, one is already included among the ranks of the Mahāyāna bodhisattvas. Because it serves as the root of unsurpassed awakening and is the natural outflow of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), it is divided into the basis for all trainings.
From this point onward, there may be those who regress or those who do not regress; it is clear that some will retreat and yet practice again, while others will regress and fail to practice.
This initial generation of the mind of awakening arises from four conditions: first, seeing or hearing that the Buddha and others possess great supernormal powers;
second, hearing the proclamation of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka teachings; [and so forth].

Third, seeing that the Dharma is about to perish, one reflects: "The Dharma, if it abides for long, can extinguish all suffering; I ought to resolve my mind [upon enlightenment] and bring about this benefit.

Fourth, seeing sentient beings in the final age and final time who are afflicted and disturbed by the ten afflictions, much ignorance, and so forth, one reflects: "In such times, it is already difficult to find those who give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles, let alone the Great Bodhi."
I shall resolve to attain enlightenment so that others may follow my example.

Furthermore, there are four causes: first, the possession of the spiritual lineage; second, being sustained by virtuous friends; third, compassion for sentient beings; and fourth, fearlessness in the face of difficult practices.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Through the power of purification, the firm mind’s superior progress, it is called the Bodhisattva’s initial cultivation over three incalculable great eons. The Great Bodhicitta takes the roots of goodness as its essence; this is termed the power of purification.
Because it subdues and eliminates the obstacles to be abandoned by taking virtuous friends as conditions, it is termed the power of superiority.
Because it is spurred on by non-retrogression and non-defeat, it is termed the power of firmness.

Even if one encounters evil friends who employ skillful means to obstruct and destroy it, one never abandons the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*); the wholesome dharmas one cultivates increase ever more and more. Such superior progress is termed the "initial production of the thought [of awakening]."

From the time after first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, the newly perfumed seeds of impure hearing and reflection distinguish and nourish the pure seeds; these two combined are termed "seeds accomplished through cultivation."
Having established a limit for the ocean of birth and death, one will before long certainly and swiftly realize the further shore; therefore, the dharmas practiced are called *pāramitās*.

There are four kinds of appropriate qualities in the spiritual friends one encounters, which one should understand and approach for study: first, they are intelligent and wise, not falling into evil views;
second, they do not teach heedlessness nor provide the tools thereof.
Third, one does not instruct others in unwholesome conduct, nor does one provide them with the conditions for such conduct;

fourth, one does not encourage the abandonment of previously cultivated superior dharmas to cultivate inferior ones, and never encourages the abandonment of the Mahāyāna to cultivate the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles.
The opposite of this constitutes the characteristics of a bad friend (*pāpamitra*), whom one should avoid.

One should extensively analyze the causes and conditions for the distinctions in the stages of generating the bodhicitta, as well as the extent of their merits and so forth; all of these are explained in detail in the fifty-seventh fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the first fascicle of the *Śīla-sūtra*, and the first fascicle of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

The section on the Stage of Practice through Understanding (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*) is divided into three major parts. First, the "Summary of the Abodes" concludes the ten stages of dwelling (*daśa-vihāra*). Second, the "Two Abodes" refers to the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*); among these, the "Abode of Purified Perfections" pertains to the first six practices, while the "Abode of Desire" pertains to the latter four practices.

Among the *pāramitās*, first, the exposition of giving constitutes the first five practices; "not dwelling on the perception of signs" constitutes the first six practices; and "the desire to dwell" constitutes four practices: the desire to obtain the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is the seventh practice;

the desire for the body of speech (*vāk-kāya*) is the eighth practice; the desire for the body of the marks of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa-kāya*) is the ninth practice; and the desire for the dharma-body of the marks of merit (*puṇya-lakṣaṇa-dharmakāya*) is the tenth practice.
Alternatively, it may be divided into four parts.

The preceding section concludes the explanation of the "Abodes of Comprehension" (*saṃgraha-vihāra*). From here begins the second [section], the "Pure Abodes of the Perfections" (*pāramitā-śuddha-vihāra*), which is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of five meanings that provide a general explanation of the subsequent abodes; second, the specific explanation of the stages of practice, namely the *caryā-pratipatti* or *adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*, which is further divided into two major sections.

The preceding section has already concluded the explanation of the "Inclusive Abodes" (*saṃgraha-vihāra*). From here below, the remaining three abodes will be explained. The text is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of five types that apply universally to all abodes; second, the specific explanation of the three abodes.

The initial section is divided into three parts: first, the indication of the five types of textual correspondence with their respective five meanings, which constitutes the structural alignment for the explanation;
second, the listing of the five names;
and third, the interpretation of their meanings.
Question:
"For what reason, among the previously mentioned 'bases of inclusion' (*saṃgraha-vastu*), are these five not individually correlated with the text? Answer:
"The principles are all present; that is to say, one should give rise to such a thought, for it reveals the meaning by way of showing the antidote that does not lose the mind.
'I shall cause all to enter nirvana without remainder' and so forth—this is the characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
This very act of causing them to enter nirvana without remainder is the sustaining (parigraha); the sustaining of the mind is precisely the aspiration (praṇidhāna)."
"In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa"—this is the establishment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

If one possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, one is not called a bodhisattva; rather, this is for the purpose of manifesting the corresponding samādhi and gathering the distracted mind.

However, since there were three questions previously and the text of the answers all possesses these three meanings, I shall first explain and correlate them with these three answers rather than correlating the text with five categories. This is not because these five meanings are absent from the preceding text; rather, they are stated according to their predominance, as explained by Vasubandhu.

The initial passage answers the first question; the passage concerning "giving" (dāna) answers the second question. This does not mean that other meanings are absent; rather, they are presented as answers according to what is predominant, and thus there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, to reflect upon and clarify the intermediate passage, it is shown to possess five meanings; since the preceding passage likewise possesses these five meanings by implication, they are not stated explicitly here.

The "counteractive according to meaning" refers to the locus of the obstacles to be abandoned; "establishment" refers to the principle to be realized. The first question concerning desire and aspiration constitutes the "sustaining"; the latter two questions concerning the corresponding samādhi and the gathering of the distracted mind constitute the "manifestation. These—the practices such as those questioned—collectively form the characteristics of the exposition. The three [remaining] questions inquire only about the counteractive practices; they omit the obstacles to be countered, the principle to be realized, and the general characteristics of the exposition because these are implied by the questions themselves, the principle is difficult to manifest, and the inquiry follows what is easy.

The answer is that all [three] are fully explained for the purpose of facilitating understanding; since the three—cessation (*prahāṇa*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*)—are all fully addressed.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other texts state: "In True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), afflictions do not arise. Now, it is clarified that by means of these three, one shall likewise attain that [state]; therefore, they should be explained according to their respective abidings.

In the commentary on the meaning, regarding what is clarified in this sutra, among the various stages of abiding (*vihāra*), that which is to be countered serves as the basis for the meaning; it is by depending upon that which is to be countered that the remedial practice is then explained.

That which can treat [the afflictions] refers to the subsequent practices such as aspiration and so forth; therefore, that which is to be treated is termed the "meaning of reliance. The conduct of the dwelling place, which is generally elucidated, constitutes the characteristics of what is explained; these characteristics of what is explained consist of the three types of practice: aspiration, resolve, and the concentration that gathers distraction.
Whenever one wishes to practice, the initial arising of aspiration serves to sustain and uphold that intention;
because it can sustain and uphold it, the practices so sustained—namely, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the gathering of the distracted mind—are able to reach fulfillment.

Within the sphere of abiding, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is that which is established; the internally realized limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is called "non-establishment. Now, because the principle of the supreme ultimate truth (*tattvārthasatya*), namely suchness (*tathatā*), is provisionally designated through verbal expression, it is termed "establishment."

The non-conceptual meditative concentration (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) which counteracts what was previously to be countered and serves as the counteragent is termed "manifestation" (*prabhāsvara*); this is precisely what is revealed by the initial mind of aspiration (*chanda-praṇidhāna-citta*) in the sutra. The ultimate goal (*abhiprāya*), the non-conceptual mind, is termed "manifestation. This also subsumes the time when [the mind] is subdued during its state of distraction; however, because it is omitted in the text, one should infer the essential nature of the concentration from what follows below. In the preceding section, aspiration and the vow were called the "grasping agent" (*parigrahaka*), whereas the non-conceptual mind that subdues the state of distraction is the "object grasped" (*parigṛhīta*).

This explains that the names [of the stages] manifest the two states of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the gathering of distraction; it demonstrates that the preceding aspiration and vow are what bring about this manifestation. Although the names differ between the earlier and later stages, the latter is presented as superior because it is more clearly revealed.

When practicing that conduct, the non-conceptual concentration is called "conjunction" (*yoga*). This concentration is the antidote to the obstacles that are to be countered; it is the concentration with which the practitioner is conjoined, it is the concentration conjoined with non-conceptual wisdom, and it is the concentration conjoined with the true object—therefore, it is named "conjunction."
Within the five yogas, four or five are subsumed; one who is able to practice them is called a *yogin*.
The commentary on the *Pāramitā-viśuddhi-pratiṣṭhā-sthāna-sūtra* divides the section on practice into two parts: first, the explanation of the five meanings to answer three questions;
second, from "For what reason the Bodhisattva does not dwell in signs" onwards, the resolution of these doubts and difficulties.

According to Vasubandhu’s commentary, the first section clarifies the practice of giving in response to the second question; the section beginning with "not dwelling on signs" answers the third question.
Within the answer to the third question, there are two parts: first, the direct answer to the question; second, from "Why is this? onwards, the explanation that resolves this doubt.

The former provides a detailed response by following the literal phrasing of the text to clarify it, while the latter provides a comprehensive response by following the underlying meaning to elucidate it; these are not contradictory, as each relies upon a single aspect of the meaning.

Within the first interpretation, which explains the five meanings in response to the three questions, the meaning is inherently complete with all five, as the treatise itself correlates them with the text.

The response to the questions is divided into two parts: first, answering the initial question regarding desire and aspiration through the three non-abidings; second, answering the latter two questions through non-abiding in signs. Within the response to the initial question, there are four points:

the "three non-abidings" constitute the underlying meaning (*artha*), while the "three types of giving" describe the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, this practice of giving is the act of gathering and sustaining, and this non-abiding is the establishment [of the practice]. One should carefully examine the text, and one will naturally attain understanding.
The meaning can be understood from the text: all three types of non-abiding rely on the meaning, as they all eliminate attachment and clinging to abiding.

The explanation of their characteristics is divided into three parts: first, a general assignment of the scriptural passages that describe these characteristics; second, an explanation of the reason why only the practice of giving (*dāna*) is discussed; and third, from the section "those various *pāramitās*," below, an explanation of the distinctions between the practices of non-abiding.

Regarding the explanation of the characteristics: the practice of giving within the three non-abidings constitutes all the characteristics that are explained. Since one should cultivate various practices after having generated the resolve for enlightenment, the practice of giving is presented as the characteristic explained subsequent to the generation of the resolve.
Next, regarding the explanation of why only the practice of giving (*dāna*) is taught, there are two parts: first, a general presentation and explanation;
second, a detailed specific explanation. This refers to the objection: "The *Bodhisattva-mārga-karma-sūtra* enumerates eighty-four thousand sublime deeds; why is it that here only giving is taught?"

Therefore, this general heading states, "Because the six pāramitās are subsumed within the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all practices of dāna. Here the text is inverted; it should rather read, "Because all practices of dāna subsume the six pāramitās within their intrinsic nature."
In this sutra, the exposition of the perfection of giving alone is already complete.
Question:
"If this is so, since even the perfection of wisdom encompasses the practice of all six perfections, why does it not simply state that a single wisdom encompasses them all?"

Answer: "Generosity is the beginning of spiritual practice; it is coarse and easy to cultivate, and its nature is vast and all-encompassing. Therefore, only this is mentioned here. Furthermore, it is both manifest and comprehensive, serving as the general title of the sutra, designated by way of its preeminent wisdom."

Answer: "The practice is named after its initial stage; however, according to the intent of the text, although hundreds of thousands of practices are mentioned, it speaks only of the donor, because giving encompasses all practices."

The previously mentioned "abiding places" (*vihāra*) refer to the ten stages (*bhūmi*); these "pure abiding places" (*viśuddha-vihāra*) of the *pāramitās*, such as the "joyful practice" (*pramuditā-caryā*) and so forth, refer to the ten practices (*caryā*). It is taught that each is cultivated in succession one by one; because this is a summary, only giving (*dāna*) is said to encompass the six perfections, rather than teaching that the practice of giving encompasses all practices.

Furthermore, there are four types of bodhisattva practice: first, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa); second, the perfections (pāramitā); third, the various supernormal powers (abhijñā); and fourth, the maturation of sentient beings. Now, by citing the first type of practice, these others are subsumed; thus, there is no contradiction.
Below, there are two parts to the detailed explanation of the text: first, the heading indicating that there are three types of giving; second, the individual explanations thereof.

Regarding these three types, they are each explained separately in Vasubandhu’s commentary (*Treatise on the Ten Stages*), and their similarities and differences are also reconciled within the *Xuanji* (Commentary by Ci’en); one should consult and examine them.
Within the gift of Dharma there are three parts: first, the enumeration; second, the manifestation of its characteristics; and third, the conclusion.

Regarding the statement "those various pāramitās have two kinds of fruits," the following explains the distinctions among the three types of non-abiding gifts within the scriptural text: first, the enumeration; second, the detailed explanation; and third, the correlation with the scripture.

In the detailed explanation of each: through giving, one obtains great merit and reward, which refers to the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) of abundant wealth; through ethical discipline, one obtains rebirth in the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, and others—noble and honorable bodies—which is the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*); through the practice of patience, one obtains great companions and a large retinue; through diligence, one obtains uninterrupted fruits; through meditative concentration, one obtains an indestructible body, both of which are dominant fruits;
and through wisdom, one obtains sharp faculties, which is the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

There are two types of results of great joy: first, the unconditioned fruit of dissociation (*asamskṛta-viśleṣa-phala*); second, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) consisting of attaining mastery within the great assembly.

There are two types of present results: first, obtaining faith, respect, and offerings, which constitute three fruits—namely, the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), the flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
In the past one gave to others, and now one receives the gifts of others; this constitutes the fruit of equal outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Second, the attainment of *dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa in the present life), which refers to the semblance of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), such as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), obtained through the six mundane practices, constituting *dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*.

"Dharma" refers to the principle; it is the principle by which one eliminates the *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness) in the present life and attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because this is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). This is because it was previously stated that [this cessation] is attained through the power of a person (*puruṣa-bala*).

Furthermore, there are five types of *dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*: first, the attainment of the pleasures of the five sensory desires in the present; the remaining four involve the induction of the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) so that they manifest before one, accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), which eliminates a portion of the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*). These are also called *dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*, and all are termed "fruits of the present."

According to what is appropriate for the results obtained from giving and the other perfections, these are allocated within the three types of "non-abiding" giving mentioned in the sutra: the future result of giving constitutes one; the future results of the remaining five perfections constitute another; and the present result constitutes yet another.

However, the five sense objects such as form (*rūpa*) are distinct from the object of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); thus, they are separated into two categories: the former because [acts such as] faith, reverence, and making offerings are subsumed under the five sense objects, and the latter because the five supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and nirvāṇa are subsumed under the object of mental phenomena.
Regarding the "explanation of inclusion," the sūtra states that one "should practice giving," which refers to the three types of giving to be practiced mentioned above.
Regarding the "explanation of establishment," "practicing giving without abiding" likewise refers to the three types of non-abiding mentioned above.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the connection to the scriptural passage; second, the explanation of the characteristics of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the phrase "because of non-abiding," it means that the absence of dwelling and attachment is the primary meaning.
Regarding "the ultimate truth (paramārtha) of things as they are": among the three kinds of giving, non-abiding is the ultimate truth.

"Things as they are" refers to the three previously mentioned forms of non-abiding in giving: first, non-abiding in the act of giving material things; second, giving without a fixed point of reference; and third, non-abiding in the six sense objects. Within all such matters, the practice of non-abiding giving is termed the ultimate truth.

Therefore, the conclusion of the treatise states: "The phrase 'the objects upon which one does not dwell, etc., and all such matters, etc. indicates that the first matter is cited, while the 'etc. includes non-dwelling and giving amidst the six sense-objects; these three types combined are termed 'all such matters.'"
Not abiding in these three things—giving, morality, and patience—is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Thus far, the practice of giving has explained the first four meanings; hereafter, the fifth meaning, which concerns meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the gathering of a distracted mind, will be explained. The text for this portion is easy to understand.

"Signs" (*nimitta*) refer to the object, and "conception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the mind. As Vasubandhu’s *Bhāṣya* states: the giver, the recipient, and the gift—these correspond to the three factors of the six perfections. To grasp these three signs is called "the conception of signs," which is precisely the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).

There are seven perversions, namely: the perversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; and the perversions of perception, mind, and view. Here, the perversion of perception is explained as encompassing the perversions of mind and view.
By contemplating the emptiness of the three factors and giving rise to the purity of the three wheels, it is called "non-abiding.

The *Nengduan* (*Prajñāpāramitā-nirdeśa*) states: "As one does not abide in the perception of signs. Since even desire and aspiration do not involve abiding attachment as described above, the same applies to the attainment of meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*) and concentration (*samādhi*), which gather and collect the distracted mind; these should be like the initial non-abiding in giving. Therefore, there is the expression "as if," or because according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) their nature is without abiding attachment, the perception of giving should abide nowhere in accordance with reality.

According to Vasubandhu’s interpretation, if one subdues the mind to eliminate hindrances, then by practicing as taught—without dwelling on the perception of signs—the obstructive mind will naturally cease.

This explanation, which fully answers the three questions according to their meaning, follows the gradual cultivation of a beginner; thus, the Master Vasubandhu provides specific answers to the three questions with increased clarity in the textual presentation, as explained above.

In the *Treatise by Vasubandhu*, the three types of non-abiding giving are explained with a distinction from this [text], stating: "One's own person, requital of gratitude, and karmic retribution—none of these are clung to. Here, "one's own person" refers to the future fruit, while "requital of gratitude" refers to the present fruit.
Although they are largely similar in their general outline, there are distinctions in what is intended; thus, while the meanings emerge from a hundred paths, they do not contradict one another.
Relying on this principle, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states: "One practices giving without attachment to one's own kind, and one practices giving without attachment to anything else," and so forth.

The preceding section explained five meanings to answer three questions, completing the interpretation of the first five lines; the subsequent section explains "Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs," thereby resolving doubts and difficulties.
Next, the sixth practice is explained. The text is divided into two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation.
Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "In this regard, there may be doubt: if one is free from the conceptualization of the marks of giving and so forth, how can one accomplish the merit of giving?"

It refers to a doubt that arises as follows: "If the three factors are not empty, then giving may bring merit; since the three factors are empty, there should be no merit in giving. Therefore, this treatise states:

"There may be some bodhisattvas who, because they crave merit, are unable to endure this. Because they practice giving out of a craving for merit, they cannot bear hearing that these three factors are empty and thus fail to practice giving and so forth. Consequently, it next asks: "For what reason?"

Subsequently, the commentary on the scriptural text is divided into three parts, while the treatise itself is divided into two: first, the explanation of the Dharma; second, the interpretation of the metaphor. The explanation of the Dharma is not further subdivided.

Within the interpretation of the metaphor, the initial point concerns giving that does not abide in signs (*nimitta*); it is like space, which is all-pervasive, because both the fruit with signs and the fruit without signs can depend upon it.
Giving that abides in signs is not so; since it cannot attain the signless, it is not all-pervasive.

Furthermore, because [the donor] gives with a mind that is expansive and free from attachment to signs (*nimitta*), when the fruit is subsequently attained, the form is high above and below; for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) Dharma transcends the three realms, and thus the form is horizontally vast and great, filling the ten directions.
It is not so with giving performed while attached to signs; when the fruit is subsequently attained, it exists only within the three realms and does not extend to the ten directions.

Alternatively, it is called "vast and expansive" because it is all-encompassing; because its subsequent causes are inexhaustible, it accords with the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), widely transporting sentient beings without end.
Abiding in signs is not so; it does not accord with ultimate truth and does not universally benefit others.

In the concluding statement of the sutra, the True Dharma (Zhendi) edition lacks the passage beginning with "but should" (*dāni yuktam*) and so forth; it agrees with the Central Indian Sanskrit manuscript, whereas other editions all contain it.
Since this treatise cites the sutra without providing an explanation [of that passage], we know that its conclusion was likewise absent.
Giving without abiding in signs yields the greatest merit; this is consistent across all versions.

Regarding the third section on the desire for abodes, this is explained based on eight abodes, which further rely on eighteen explanations. Within this, there are two parts: first, the desire to attain the form-body (*rūpakāya*), which constitutes the seventh practice; second, the desire to attain the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which comprises the final three practices.
The initial scriptural passage consists of three parts: first, the question; second, the answer; and third, the establishment.
Within the question, there are two sections: the basis of meaning and the description of characteristics.
Within the establishment, there are three aspects: sustaining, establishing, and manifesting.
The answer contains nothing at all [contradictory], because the meaning of the text is no different from its beginning to its end, and it is taken as the Buddha’s own teaching.

For those who wish to attain the dwelling place of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), many beginner bodhisattvas practice with signs; upon suddenly hearing of signless giving purified of the three spheres, they immediately give rise to doubt and confusion. This is because, for example, the body of Śākyamuni Buddha already possesses the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; thus one knows that a cause of giving with signs will, in turn, result in a fruit with signs.
The *Devatāputra-śāstra* asks: "How does doubt arise?
'If one practices giving without abiding in dharmas, how can one practice giving for the sake of the Buddha's bodhi?'"

Since he takes the body of Śākyamuni, subject to arising and ceasing, as the basis for awakening, and attains it by practicing conditioned giving, if he were instead to practice the cause of the non-abiding dharma through signless practice, he should have attained that fruit of non-abiding signs; how then could he attain this fruit of arising and ceasing?

In this treatise, it is not because there is doubt; rather, it is because it speaks of the practitioner at the initial stage of training, who has not yet realized the signless (animitta) and thus practices with signs as a cause, aspiring for the state of Buddhahood.

Śākyamuni possesses a body subject to arising and ceasing; this is because it is a physical body (*rūpakāya*) endowed with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*). Since this body of marks serves as the supreme basis for the awakening (*bodhi*) of a Buddha, the treatise states: "One who desires to obtain the physical body."

The intent of that treatise is explained as follows: because the preceding discussion on the cause of signless giving gave rise to doubt, the subsequent sutra passage serves to resolve that very doubt.

The intent of this treatise is as follows: because beginners practice giving with signs in order to obtain the "sign-endowed" body of Śākyamuni and others, they take that manifested sign-body to be the true body itself. Believing that they have attained a small measure of merit, they claim it to be the true body and the substance of great merit; therefore, it is said that they do so "desiring to obtain the form-body (rūpakāya)."

To counteract pride regarding the physical body and attain a body possessing even a few marks of merit—namely, the conceit that one has attained a body of truly manifold merits—is overweening pride (*adhimāna*). To shatter this pride, there is the following sutra.

Therefore, combining the two treatises, the preceding text of the two vehicles identifies the delusion of birth as "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) and the false appearance of what is desired as "pride" (*māna*). To destroy these two delusions of doubt and pride, the subsequent sutra is taught.

For a beginner practitioner who is of either determinate or indeterminate lineage and is a Mahāyāna ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), doubt and perplexity constitute the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) as well as the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

For a beginner practitioner who is a noble one (*ārya*) having generated the resolve for enlightenment, both hindrances are simultaneously addressed: those still in training (*śaikṣa*) address the afflictive hindrance, while those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) address only the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Just as Śāriputra, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, finally severed his doubts, regrets, and afflictions such as sorrow, so it is here as well.

Precisely because of the meaning explained above, people fail to realize that Vasubandhu’s treatise does not contradict Asaṅga’s teaching; one should examine this carefully, for these two works are in agreement and truly do not conflict.

Therefore, Vasubandhu stated: "From this point onward, all the sūtras manifest the severing of the arising of doubt. Thus we know that his treatise, based on the preceding discourse, addresses the doubts that arise in beginners; it produces the subsequent scriptural passages to refute those doubts.

This treatise, however, is based on the fact that beginners might hope for qualities that are not truly real while practicing; it produces the subsequent scriptural passages to refute such pride. Therefore, there is no contradiction between them.
Furthermore, that treatise, based on the fact that beginners with sharp faculties often give rise to doubts regarding the past, explains the Sūtra below;
this treatise, based on the fact that beginners with dull faculties often give rise to pride regarding the future, explains the Sūtra below.

Furthermore, in that treatise, the three preceding sections are formulated according to the expansion of the literal phrasing to answer three questions; thus, they employ distinct principles to generate the subsequent sutra as a means of resolving doubts.

In this present treatise, however, the meaning is fully comprehensive such that each section answers all three questions; therefore, it does not employ different principles to generate the subsequent sutra, but rather teaches it for the purpose of eliminating pride. In reality, these two approaches are not contradictory.
Furthermore, that [preceding] sutra was taught because beginners harbor doubts based on the refutation of indeterminate afflictions;
this sutra was taught because it enables beginners to sever the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) regarding determinate afflictions.
The four points mentioned above are based on the perspective of commonality (*sādharmya*) to harmonize the two treatises.
From the perspective of difference (*vaidharmya*), there are furthermore four points.

This treatise, being intended for those who delight in extensive exposition, explains three stages—from the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up to the Buddha—fully describing them all; it provides detailed answers in every passage, thereby giving rise to the textual expression of "arrogance" (*māna*).
That treatise, for the sake of those who prefer to hear a brief summary, provides separate answers to the three questions and subsequently resolves all doubts.

Furthermore, this treatise is intended for those of sharp faculties who attain awakening upon hearing it once; thus it explains the three stages in a single cycle of discourse, providing comprehensive answers throughout the text. The arising of pride and the subsequent composition of the text differ in their sequence [from the other].

That treatise, however, is intended for those of duller faculties who understand only after hearing it a second time; therefore, it explains it in two cycles, providing separate answers to the three questions while the remainder serves to dispel doubts.
Furthermore, this treatise was taught for those of sharp faculties who have come at the beginning of the teaching during a single cycle; therefore, it speaks of the arising of conceit.
That treatise was taught for those of dull faculties who have come later during two cycles; therefore, it speaks of the destruction of doubt.
Furthermore, principles emerge in a hundred ways; why labor for a single penetration?

Their refutations of attachments and generation of pride differ from one another. Within a single assembly, there are preferences for the extensive or the concise; faculties are either sharp or dull; what is heard may be singular or repeated; and principles may be thoroughly penetrated in various ways. Because these diverse distinctions exist, the interpretations in the two treatises differ.

It is not so; how could Asaṅga have deviated from Maitreya, or Vasubandhu have differed from his venerable elder brother, when Asaṅga received the verses from Maitreya and subsequently entrusted them to Vasubandhu, commanding him to compose a commentary?

The opening verse of homage in Asaṅga’s treatise states: "The teachings and their meanings as expounded by the Wise One—I, having heard them, shall now explain them for you. Thus, we know that the one who says, "having heard them, I shall explain them for you," is Maitreya, the author of these verses.

The verses explained in Vasubandhu’s commentary were composed by Maitreya; thus, Vasubandhu’s own verse states: "I prostrate to the body of incomparable merit, whose great wisdom has fully realized the teachings and instructs us. This is identical to the expression of reverence at the beginning of this treatise. One should understand it as previously explained regarding the three questions and the summary of the abodes (*sthāna-saṃgraha*), for all of these should be stated here.
By means of this, one should reach a definitive understanding by correlating it with the various scriptural passages that follow.

Regarding the subsequent text, one should merely explain its textual characteristics; furthermore, when proceeding to correlate and explain the treatise (śāstra), one should follow the threefold method used for explaining the scriptures.

The initial explanation of the text of the question contains two parts: first, an interpretation of the meaning based on the sūtra; second, an explanation of the characteristics according to the śāstra.
Herein, [the term] "complete" (paripūrṇa) refers to the fulfillment [of the path] as translated by Paramārtha; the meaning is identical, though the names differ.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "The excellence of all marks" refers to the accomplishment of conditioned marks (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
Because it is the Buddha’s body of awakening (*bodhi-kāya*), it is fully accomplished; this is the direct translation of the term.
As for "excellence" (*viśeṣa-guṇa*), conditioned marks serve as the substance of the Buddha's excellent qualities; this is the meaning-based translation.

Regarding the observation of the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*) below—referring to the primary and secondary marks—the commentary by Vasubandhu explains them as four marks; that is, because they consist of the three marks of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), the mark of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is not mentioned, as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Subhūti, intuitively grasping the Buddha’s intention, said: "It is not so. One cannot perceive the true body of the Buddha through the accomplishment of the three marks of the conditioned; what has been described as the conditioned does not possess the characteristics of the Dharma-body.

Regarding the characteristics of the Dharma-body: taking the signless as its characteristic, because the characteristics of the three realms of existence are conditioned characteristics, one practices the cause of the signless and thereby attains the fruit of the unconditioned, signless, and true Dharma-body; it is not by practicing the cause of the signless that one obtains the conditioned, sign-possessing, and provisional transformation body or reward body.
Subsequently, in order to fulfill the meaning of the preceding inquiry and provide the next level of response, the Buddha addresses him again. This section is divided into three parts.
First: "Whatever has marks is entirely illusory. This establishes the aspiration and vow, revealing that conditioned marks are illusory;
by contrast, it clarifies that the markless mark which differs from this illusion is not [illusory].

This is false; it causes one to grasp and subsequently give rise to desire and aspiration, rather than desire and aspiration grasping and holding onto the falsely imagined phenomena of signs (*nimitta*).
These falsely imagined phenomena with signs are not non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*).
Regarding the two types of practice involving grasping, the intention of desire and aspiration refers to the deluded practice of those beginners who harbor the evil desire and aspiration for signs.
This is not that the wishless aspiration of *prajñā* is itself wishless;

rather, because the wishless aspiration of *prajñā* seeks the wishless, the treatise states that this wishful aspiration sustains the concentration of the wishless (*animitta-samādhi*). It is the fundamental wishful aspiration that gathers together the two distracted minds;
therefore, this wishful aspiration constitutes the sequential process of the wishless aspiration for one who practices correctly.

The second says: "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then they are not false. This establishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Here, "marks" refers to the false transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while "non-marks" refers to the true Dharma body (*dharmakāya*). If one sees that the various conditioned marks of the transformation body are not the marklessness of the Dharma body, then they are not false. For those [who hold otherwise], taking the marked transformation body to be the mark of the true body is therefore false.

Regarding the third bond mentioned later: all manifested forms possess characteristics and are not truly formless. Thus, one perceives the Dharmakāya Tathāgata; this is what is meant by "manifestation. This is precisely the time when the previously described non-discriminative samādhi and the gathering of scattered thoughts occur. Within these possessed forms, it is not that one sees the true characteristics of the Dharmakāya, yet through them, one perceives the Tathāgata.
This contemplation on seeing the Tathāgata should be verified by consulting the "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata" in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.

Regarding the subsequent explanation of the desire to abide, based on the eighteen abodes mentioned previously, the text is divided into two parts: first, explaining the desire to attain the Dharma-body of speech; second, explaining the desire to attain the Dharma-body itself.

If one wishes to attain the Dharma-body, although cause and fruit are distinct, because the essence of the True Dharma-body is that upon which all meritorious qualities depend, both the three bodies of the Buddha-fruit and the causal merit and wisdom are subsumed within the Dharma-body. Verbal teachings and sounds are not the Dharma-body itself; however, the causes of the Dharma-body are also termed the "Dharma-body."

As it is said regarding Prajñā: the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and contemplative observation (vipaśyanā) are precisely Prajñā itself; furthermore, the Prajñā of words (vyañjana-prajñā), which can give rise to and manifest [this wisdom], is also called Prajñā.
This is also the case here: because syllables can manifest and give rise to the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), speech is likewise called the Dharma-body.

The name "syllable-prajñā" (vyañjana-prajñā) is established based on the function of the signifier (*vācaka*) in relation to that which it depends upon (*vācya*). The name "Dharma-body of speech" is established based on the harmony between the essence and function of both the signifier and the signified; it is called "speech" because it is the conjunction of sound and name.
Question:

"For what reason was it stated previously that desiring to obtain the form-body (rūpakāya) is called pride (māna), yet in the subsequent passage below, desiring to obtain the dharma-body (dharmakāya) is not so called?"
Answer: "To desire to obtain the form-body as the true body is entirely contrary to principle; therefore, it is called pride (*māna*).

To desire to obtain the dharma-body does not contradict principle; although doubt may arise due to what was previously said, it is not entirely contrary to principle, and thus it is not given the name 'pride'."

Because the subsequent passage beginning with "desiring to obtain the form-body" (*rūpakāya*) does not refer to being separated from obstacles, but merely to the desire for attainment—and since it is not a doubt regarding an ultimate obstacle—it is said that desiring to obtain the form-body is a dharma that constitutes an obstacle of pride (*māna*).
If one were to claim that the Dharma-body is distinct from the dharmas that are not obstacles to pride, it would not be granted the name "freedom from obstacles.

In Vasubandhu’s commentary, this is established to dispel doubts and leads into the following scriptural passage: what was previously described as practicing giving without abiding is the profound meaning of the cause; next, the teaching that the Dharma-body does not possess the characteristics of the conditioned is the profound meaning of the result. Since the cause is profound and the result is remote, their underlying significance is difficult to comprehend.
In the future, at the time when the Semblance Dharma is about to perish, will sentient beings of that evil age be able to give rise to faith?

There is no need to doubt their faith during the preceding era of the True Dharma; however, regarding the sentient beings of the evil age in the Final Dharma, they will neither believe nor be deluded. I ask only this: will they be able to give rise to faith at the time when the Semblance Dharma is about to perish?

This was spoken during the time of the True Dharma when one practices the ten dharma-activities; it is not because the Final Dharma is superior, for the practices of precept, concentration, and wisdom therein are all not preeminent. Therefore, this inquiry is made; since there are no longer those who train in the three studies during the Final Dharma, such a question is not raised.

That treatise raises doubts based on the preceding text, whereas this treatise relies on the cause—the desire to attain the *dharmakāya* through speech—to realize the foundation of the *dharmakāya*. Since it will circulate in the world in the future as a sutra revealed after [the Buddha's] passing, there is no contradiction between them.
The text is divided into three parts: first, the correlation with the scriptural passage; second, the explanation of the question; and third, the explanation of the answer.

Regarding the phrase "desiring to attain the Dharma-body of speech," this clarifies the purpose for which the scripture was delivered: Subhūti heard that the profound and wondrous Dharma is difficult to know through its true nature (*dharmatā*). While it is understandable that [the Buddha] would be so [in his presence], one must consider whether there are many who believe now that the time, the capacity, the afflictions, and the practice have been proven superior. Is it possible that after the Buddha’s passing, there might still be those capable of faith?
Because the time, the faculties, the afflictions, and the practices are all not superior [in that future age],

Subhūti, wishing to obtain this teaching so that the Dharma-body might circulate in the world both in the present and in the future, asks whether those born in the evil world of the future evil age will be able to believe it.

Anticipating the Buddha’s response that [the Dharma-body] exists, [the author] argues: "If it is difficult even for those in the final age to have deep faith, how much more so now? For what reason do you not believe?
Thus, the following passage is introduced to demonstrate that one desires to attain the Dharma-body through the teaching of the Dharma.
The initial text has two parts: first, the correlation with the sūtra; second, the resolution of difficulties.

Within the resolution of difficulties, the phrase "the statement of the sūtra-words" (*sūtrapada*) means that for all meanings, the words (*pada*) serve as the expressive medium (*vācaka*), while the exposition of the seven phrases refers to the principles being expressed. This is what Paramārtha, Paramārtha (Jinatrāta), Kumārajīva, and others refer to as "chapters and sentences" (*varga-pada*); it clarifies the principles elucidated by the meaningful sentences, which here are termed "statements."

The *Nengduan jing* (Sutra on the Ability to Sever) states: "The scriptural phrases concerning 'form' (*rūpa*). Here, "form" carries the sense of a category; it refers to the categories of meaning being explained. This does not refer solely to this *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, but includes all such works as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* within the scope of the inquiry; therefore, it is termed "the category of form."

The "phrases of the sūtras" refer to the teachings that express [the meaning]; this refers to whether the phrases of the sūtras, which are the expressive means for this category of meaning, will be able to engender faith in the evil ages of the future.
This has two intentions: first, clarifying the causes for lack of faith; second, formally posing the question.
There are two causes for lack of faith: first, the corruption of the times; second, the profundity of the sutra.

As for the corruption of the times, evil arises; as for the profundity of the sutra, it concerns the true mark (*dharmatā*). Regarding these phrases of the sutra, do you perhaps give rise to faith and understanding that they constitute the true mark?

To raise a question for the sake of correct clarification, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* (True Reality Sūtra) is titled "The Aspect of True Reality," while this [text] and the *Prajñāpāramitā-nāma-aṣṭasāhasrikā* (The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines) ask: "Do you form the notion of true reality?"
The Sūtra states that what accords with correct principle is called "the reality. Within this Sūtra, has there arisen any conceptual understanding of reality?
As for "conceptualization," does the capacity of faith to grasp an image take that which is believed to be the appearance of reality as its object?
Kumārajīva said: "Does he truly believe?
This differs in wording but is identical in meaning.

In the text of the Śāriputra-parivarta, Subhūti asks this question because he considers that since evil replaces evil in birth, and the meaning of the sutra is so profound and subtle that no one is able to believe it, he therefore poses this inquiry.

The commentary asks about the intent of the question and explains that the Buddha’s answer has two parts: first, a general response regarding existence, which the World-Honored One provides as a refutation of [the opponent's] position;
second, a detailed explanation of the meaning of existence.

The separate explanation of the meaning is divided into two parts: first, a detailed and specific explanation of the meaning of "existence" (*sat*); second, an explanation of the essential meaning of the *dharmakāya*, beginning with the passage "For this reason... and so forth.

The initial passage is further divided into two parts: first, an extensive explanation of the sūtra; second, the correlation of the fivefold meanings starting from the phrase "the true nature (*dharmatā*) that shall arise therein.

The first part is divided into two sections: first, the explanation of "there being a time" (*kāla*); second, the explanation of "there being a cause" (*hetu*), as well as the explanation of how, by virtue of this, the true nature can arise.
Regarding the phrase "when the True Dharma is about to perish," this refers to the time when its practice gradually vanishes; this is one interpretation.

Subhūti asks generally about the difficulty of faith in the future, while the World-Honored One answers specifically that there will be faith in the sūtras during the period when practice is about to perish. By contrast, he reveals that previously there were many who had faith, characterized by having the teaching, having the practice, and having the realization of the fruit—this is called the True Dharma.
Having the teaching and the practice, but not attaining the realization of the fruit, is called the Semblance Dharma.
The period in which there is only the teaching and no further practice is called the Dharma of the Final Age (*paścimadharma*).

However, according to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, it is calculated in five-hundred-year intervals: in the first five hundred years, liberation is firm; in the second five hundred years, meditative concentration is firm; in the third five hundred years, learning is firm; in the fourth five hundred years, merit is firm; and in the fifth five hundred years, contention is firm.

The Hīnayāna does not rely on five hundred years for its chronological correlation; as seen in the *Upadeśa on the Sūtra of the Duration of the True Dharma*, various traditions, and the *Mahāmāyā-sūtra* and others, the matters recorded by the Buddha are correlated only with periods of one hundred or two hundred years.
Now, relying on the Mahāyāna, this sutra speaks of "the final five hundred years," because it allocates [the duration of the Dharma] in periods of five hundred years.

Regarding the Buddha’s teachings, the periods of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), and the Final Dharma are all termed the "True Dharma"; it is not that only the initial period, characterized by realization and liberation, is called the True Dharma.
If even those who have attained liberation find it difficult [to understand], how much more so for those lacking faith?
Therefore, he did not provide an answer.

The Buddha initially prophesied that the True Dharma (*saddharma*) would endure for one thousand years, the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*) for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma (*antardhānadharma*) for ten thousand years; however, due to his ordination of women, the duration of the True Dharma was reduced to only five hundred years.

Regarding this, there are two explanations. One says that the True Dharma will now last for only five hundred years; because women were permitted to enter the order, the duration was reduced by five hundred years. Although the Eight Rules of Respect were taught, they did not prevent the reduction of the True Dharma’s lifespan; because those rules were not practiced, the True Dharma has returned to extinction.
Therefore, as the Sūtras state and as the Sarvāstivāda and other schools maintain, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) alone lasts for five hundred years.

According to their interpretation, the "time when the True Dharma is about to perish" refers to the period when practice gradually declines; it does not refer to the earlier period, because during the first five hundred years there was liberation and practice flourished, nor does it refer to the later period, because at that time practice had already ceased to exist.

Now, when it is said that the practice of cultivation is gradually about to perish, this refers to the third five-hundred-year period; within these one thousand years of the Semblance Dharma (*sāṃketika-dharma*), it is during the final five hundred years that the practice will gradually vanish. Even in such an evil age, there are still those who will give rise to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) regarding the sūtras, let alone those in earlier stages who lack faith.
From this point onward, times became distant and people grew corrupt, with few developing faith; therefore, the sutras do not speak of it.

Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā-nirvedha* states: "In the later time, the later period, during the final five hundred years, when the True Dharma is about to perish and the era is shifting. Here, the "later time" refers to the first five hundred years;
the "later period" refers to the second five hundred years.
"The latter five hundred years" refers to the third five-hundred-year period, which is the time when the practice of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is about to perish.

According to a second explanation, the True Dharma lasts for one thousand years; if the Eight Respectful Precepts (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) were not taught, there would be no practitioners at all and the True Dharma would be on the verge of extinction. Since there are indeed practitioners, the True Dharma remains established through meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The Mahāsāṃghika school and others all maintain this view.

If one follows that teaching, it refers to the fourth five-hundred-year period, known as the time when practice gradually begins to perish; if even during such a degenerate age one can still give rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), how much more so for those in earlier stages who lack faith?
In later ages of decline, those who give rise to faith will be few; therefore, the sutras do not speak of them.

When the *Śataśāstra* (The Treatise on the Severance of Doubt) refers to "later times," it indicates the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and not merely the time while the Buddha was still in office.

As for the term "subsequent portion" (*paścādbhāga*), it clarifies that this is not within the first millennium of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), which is the period when one could still realize the fruits of the path.

When it is said "in the final five hundred years," this refers to the time when practice is about to perish within the one-thousand-year period of the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka), and not to the initial five hundred years when practice is flourishing.
This subsequent period is divided into four parts: first, the "later time," which refers to the first five hundred years;
second, the "subsequent part," which refers to the next five hundred years;
third, the "last five hundred years," which refers to the third five hundred years.

Fourth: Regarding the period when the True Dharma is about to perish, specifically during the fourth five-hundred-year period—that is, the time following the practice of the True Dharma when it is on the verge of extinction—there are two interpretations, resulting in different scriptural accounts.

Paramārtha and Kumārajīva both generally and collectively speak of the future末法 (mòfǎ) age, failing to recognize the profound meaning of the "three periods after" [the Buddha's passing]. Therefore, the *Tattvasaṃgraha-sūtra* states, "the present time and the future world," which they have taken as an error; for it does not inquire about a superior period, but rather about a degenerate period.

Furthermore, it is said: "In the future age, during the final five hundred years. Here, taking one as ten, five hundred becomes fifty; this is not contradictory, for mathematicians possess such a method of calculation.
The first part explains "existence at a time," while the second explains "existence by cause," as well as explaining how the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) arises therefrom.
This section is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying that the true nature arises because there are four causes; second, correlating these individually with the sutra text.

Regarding the four causes: immediately prior to that time, the Buddha taught that within such an evil age there are four manifest causes. First, long cultivation of the practices of the three trainings; second, encountering the Buddha and accumulating superior causes; third, being sustained by the Buddha’s grace; and fourth, although lacking the three trainings, the accumulation of causes, and the Buddha’s sustenance, one is still able to give rise to faith by virtue of being endowed with the karmic fruit of merit. Thus, for such a person, there is no obstacle to the Dharma, and through the convergence of merit, faith arises.
The evil age is able to produce the realization of the true nature (*dharmatā*) within the teachings of that true nature due to four causes. According to the intent of Vasubandhu’s commentary:

because there will be bodhisattvas in future ages who internally possess the virtues of the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), and because these bodhisattvas externally encounter favorable conditions, planting the three kinds of causes in the presence of the Buddhas—it should be known that such persons can produce the realization of the true nature. Therefore, the verse says: "In that evil age, when the bodhisattva is fully endowed with the three virtues, it is not in vain, for the reality exists. That is to say, the Buddha fully perceives and knows these bodhisattvas: that they uphold the precepts, cultivate merit, and take birth through the accumulation of merit; and that by virtue of their wisdom, the Buddha fully perceives and knows them to be free from the eight and forty faults of attachment to persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-abhiniveśa*).
The Sūtra states that "possessing precepts and possessing merit" clarifies the practice of cultivation.
First, the text is correlated with the scriptural passage; second, it is explained point-by-point in response to difficulties. Within this, the three trainings have four tracks:

non-attachment and non-hatred are the tracks of the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*); right mindfulness is the track of the training in concentration (*samādhi*); and right concentration is the track of the training in wisdom (*prajñā*). Because the Three Piṭakas provide different explanations based on the three faculties, only these three trainings are mentioned here.

Furthermore, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the cause for emerging from the evil realms; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the cause for emerging from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); and wisdom (*prajñā*) is the cause for emerging from the three realms.
Moreover, *śrāvakas* primarily study ethical discipline, *pratyekabuddhas* primarily practice meditative concentration, and *bodhisattvas* primarily study wisdom.
Furthermore, ethical discipline (*śīla*) can eliminate unwholesome causes; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can cultivate wholesome causes; and wisdom (*prajñā*) can benefit sentient beings.
Moreover, ethical discipline attains a superior physical basis; meditative concentration can distance one from evil; and wisdom can encompass wholesome causes.
The three trainings are taught for various distinct reasons such as these; one should consult the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* for further details.
Regarding the "virtues," these begin with qualities such as having few desires and extend up to states such as samādhi; this is explained according to the sequence of difficulties.

As stated in the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Bequeathed Teaching), there are six aspects of upholding the precepts, which correspond to the six branches of yoga: first, upholding the precepts; second, restraining the mind; third, knowing the proper measure; fourth, shame and remorse; fifth, patience; and sixth, a straightforward mind. All of these are subsumed within the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).

Right concentration also consists of six factors, as the first six are subsumed within the *Aṣṭamahāpuruṣavīthi* (The Eight Arousals of a Great Man): first, fewness of desires; second, contentment; third, seclusion; fourth, diligence; fifth, non-delusive mindfulness; and sixth, right concentration.
Right wisdom encompasses two aspects: first, wisdom; second, non-proliferation (*aprapañca*).
The precepts and wisdom are easy to maintain and thus are not explained at length;
the characteristics of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) are obscure, and therefore they are explained in detail.

Regarding the term "merit" (*guṇa*), it is spoken of as being all-encompassing; thus, within the *Eight Arousals of the Great Persons*, beginning with few desires and ending with equanimity (*upekṣā*), these six dharmas are subsumed as merit. Of these, the first six and the latter two pertain respectively to morality (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). One should further consult the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and the *Sūtra on the Eight Arousals of the Great Persons* to correlate them with the *Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching*. Those who possess the three trainings take the sūtras as their reality, for since the teachings accord with principle, they are able to give rise to faith; this faith is itself the mark of reality.
2. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Sūtra says, 'Having already obtained offerings,'" etc., the following explains the accumulation of superior causes.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the correlation with the Sūtra text; second, the explanation of each difficulty.
By encountering various Buddhas, two kinds of causes are accumulated: first, material offerings; second, practice-based offerings.
Practice-based offerings consist of planting roots of goodness.
Regarding material offerings, the sutra simply refers to them as "cultivation of offering.

There are ten types of offering: first, manifest; second, non-manifest; third, both manifest and non-manifest; fourth, one's own; fifth, another's; sixth, both; seventh, material and reverential; eighth, vast; ninth, untainted—these nine aforementioned types are termed "cultivation of offering" in the sutra;
tenth, the offering of right practice, which here is termed "planting all roots of goodness."
These ten causes are collectively termed the "causes of origination.
To resolve this difficulty, it is explained: if even a single mind of pure faith can produce such karma, how much more so for one who gives rise to the true mark (*dharmatā*)?

This interpretation of the scriptural passage concerning the phrase "even a single moment of pure faith" does not mean that one can generate a single moment of faith in the sutra merely by encountering a few Buddhas. On the contrary, it reveals that it is only through encountering and making offerings to ten million Buddhas and thereby cultivating roots of goodness that one can generate even a single moment of faith in the sutra; for such faith is difficult to produce.

Therefore, it is not the case that at the beginning of the sutra one makes offerings to few Buddhas and only later reveals that it is by making offerings to a great many Buddhas [that one attains this]. If even the karma of a single thought of pure faith arises from having universally made offerings to many Buddhas in previous lives, how much more so for those who extensively give rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) regarding this sutra—could they not have encountered and made offerings to many Buddhas in previous lives?

Beginning with the ability to give rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) through extensive sūtras and ending with a single moment of pure faith in even a few phrases of a sūtra, the intermediate stages of practice and lack of faith are omitted; thus it is said "even down to" and "even a single instance of faith," for this still presupposes having encountered and made offerings to many Buddhas in the past—how much more so for one who gives rise to extensive faith?
III. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Sūtra says, 'The Tathāgata knows all,'" etc., this is the third section, explaining what is embraced by the Buddha.
It is divided into two parts: first, an expository analysis; second, a word-by-word correlation with the text.

They appear to be distinct in order to clarify the differentiation of the mind: that which knows is called the "name-body" (nāmakāya), while the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) knows the four aggregates;
that which sees is the "form-body" (rūpakāya), while the five sensory consciousnesses know the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).

Because he knows the three types of action through his majestic deportment, it is said that he knows "all. Among walking, standing, and performing activities, he knows their minds and perceives their basis.

Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "The Buddha does not know by seeing the fruit; rather, he perceives it directly through the power of his vow-knowledge (*praṇidhijñāna*). This means that the Buddha does not infer [the mind] by seeing its result, because he perceives it directly through the manifestation of his vow-knowledge.

The term "thoroughly knowing" (*parijñā*) excludes what is seen by the eye, while the term "thoroughly seeing" (*sākṣād-darśana*) excludes what is known through inference; it is to prevent these two [misconceptions] that both "knowing" and "seeing" are taught.

However, while all other versions contain only these two—thoroughly knowing and thoroughly seeing—the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra*) contains three, adding "thoroughly awakening" (*paribodha*).
The *Treatise* by Maitreya is complete, whereas the original sutra is abbreviated.

The *Treatise* states: "One who seeks offerings and respect cannot speak [of this]. He himself explains this, saying: If a person desires to obtain offerings and respect, they will claim for themselves that they possess the precepts and so forth; such a person cannot speak for themselves of their own ability to give rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is because such a person considers themselves wise and gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

To distinguish them from those [others], the text states that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to the fact that such persons merely possess the name of "possessing precepts" and so forth; the Buddha thoroughly knows that they are able to give rise to pure faith within this sūtra.

Since the treatise provides a comprehensive explanation, we know that the sūtra is concise; only within the *Nengduan jing* (Sutra on the Severance of All Doubts) are these three types of perfection (*siddhi*) fully present. Furthermore, in the lower section of Paramārtha’s translation, within the passage concerning "detachment from the flavor of tranquility," there are likewise three types of perfection. By inferring from the latter, one should understand that the former must also possess these perfections. These points manifest the inclusion by a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and they are to be correlated with the text of the sūtra.
IV. Regarding the passage, "The sūtra says that one generates and takes up an immeasurable accumulation of merit," etc., this explains the fourth [point], the gathering and maintaining of merit.
First, the correlation with the sūtra; second, the explanation following the objections.

In the Sūtra, these are mentioned separately as "producing such [merit]" and "taking up such [merit]"; here they are cited together, hence it is said that one produces and takes up immeasurable merit.
To resolve this difficulty, it is explained: "Producing refers to the time when merit is actually arising," meaning merit is produced through its current manifestation.

"Taking up refers to the time of its cessation, because the seeds are maintained," meaning that although the actual performance of meritorious deeds no longer occurs now, because the seeds of merit previously created persist, once the manifestation has ceased, there remain within the person only the maintained seeds.
Therefore, Vasubandhu stated: "That which produces is the producing cause (*janaka-hetu*)," meaning that active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) which perfumes is called the producing cause;

"that which appropriates is the sense of the fruit consisting of the perfumed self-substance," meaning that once the active manifestation has ceased, there remains only the self-substance of the seeds thus perfumed, which is the sense of the fruit produced by the producing cause of the active manifestation.
The two treatises do not differ, or perhaps that treatise reverses this statement.

However, observing the intent of the sutra: when the Semblance Dharma is about to perish, there will be sentient beings who uphold the precepts and so forth born during that time who can give rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This means that even in an evil age, there are evil sentient beings who, though they do not express a vow to be reborn there, are nonetheless able to give rise to the true mark.

“The *Lotus Sūtra* states that if one practices the ten dharma-activities during an evil age and acts in accordance with the Dharma, one should know that this person is a great bodhisattva born through the power of their vows. How could it be that the *Lotus Sūtra* is superior to this *Prajñāpāramitā*?”
"Is that the 'Maintenance of Birth through Aspiration,' or is this the 'Maintenance of Birth in Reality'?
He replied:
"That treatise concerns the Semblance Age; this treatise concerns the Final Dharma."

Furthermore, this [sūtra] corresponds to that [sūtra] in its aspiration for rebirth, and that corresponds to this in its actual practice; since both emerged during the two periods of the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma, they manifest as mutual reflections of one another. Thus, the two sūtras are no different, for both are profoundly subtle and wondrous.

Furthermore, this [text] speaks of generating pure faith in a single moment, while that [text] speaks of being able to extensively receive and uphold [the teachings]; if one upholds even a single phrase, both [texts] truly state that birth [in the Pure Land] occurs;
if one can uphold them extensively, both likewise vow that birth shall occur.
Furthermore, this sutra is composed directly and with ultimate reality, while that sutra is composed indirectly and with the aspiration for rebirth; thus, they do not contradict one another.

Regarding the passage in the sutra beginning with "These bodhisattvas," etc., the following explains how the notion of reality arises. The text is divided into three parts: first, a general correlation with the sutra; second, a detailed interpretation of the sutra text; and third, a further explanation of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

In another interpretation of the sūtra, because there are two instances of "For what reason? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) in the sūtra, the treatise is likewise divided into two parts. The first "For what reason?

interrogates and clarifies the basis for the previous statement that the three trainings (*śikṣā*) and so forth are capable of producing the true nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*). The latter "For what reason? clarifies that the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) and the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) persist as accompanying tendencies.
The initial section further divides into two parts: first, clarifying the remedies for the five kinds of wrong grasping, which specifically corresponds to the scriptural text;
second, explaining the purpose of the passage regarding the phrase "in this context, it is clearly shown that there are those who possess ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth."
The initial section has three parts: first, the heading; second, the exposition; and third, the conclusion.

Regarding the statement "the five grasping-aggregates" (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*): the first three are distinguished as grasping with respect to the person, while the latter two are distinguished as grasping with respect to the objects; thus, they are combined into five attachments. Although there are four types of persons, they are collectively described as one "non-existent" [self]; therefore, they are explained here in combination.

In Vasubandhu’s treatise, the distinctions are analyzed based on the perceptions of grasping and formations; thus, eight meanings are established, as there are four types each for the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Since non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) frequently give rise to conceptual discrimination, calculating the three periods of time and so forth, and clinging to a real self, all four forms of the grasping at a self are designated as belonging to the non-Buddhists.
"Transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) means "arising," for it arises from the grasping of conceptualizations.

Ordinary beings within our own school remain at a lower level; likewise, Śrāvakas and others mostly grasp at the existence of phenomena. A certain class of Bodhisattvas who attain sudden enlightenment, as well as those of indeterminate lineage who have turned toward the Mahāyāna, mostly grasp at the emptiness of phenomena; this is termed "overweening pride."

These three are established based on persons to distinguish their modes of grasping: the first is the grasping at a self, while the latter two are the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Phenomenal grasping is subsumed under existence and emptiness; it consists in grasping the subject and object as existent, because one grasps the two natures as non-existent.

The meditative absorption on the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the world is called "functioning with signs" (*animitta-vṛtti*). The lower dhyānas, the entirety of the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and a small portion of the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) are called "absorption with perception" (*saṃjñā-samādhi*).
