Regarding the correspondence with the textual structure of the "Sixfold Endowments" in the *Tathāgatagotra-parivarta* of this sutra, that sutra further states: "In the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Tathāgata, all subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are completely and correctly severed, and [the Tathāgata] possesses mastery and unimpededness regarding all phenomena. This reveals that one enters the stage of the Tathāgata by means of the final subtle obstacles; thus, it is said that on the Buddha-stage two delusions are severed, and having completed their severance, one becomes a Buddha—this is the summary statement.
That sutra further states: "The Tathāgata, at the second stage, establishes the instructions for śrāvakas and institutes the Three Vehicles.

At the fourth stage, the Tathāgata expounds the eighty-four thousand clusters of Dharma and subdues the four Māras. These two stages refer to the establishment of the Great Dharma herein; when establishing the Great Dharma, he instructs the Three Vehicles to cultivate the Right Path, subdues the four Māras, and causes them to abandon what is erroneous.

That sutra further states: "The Tathāgata, in the fifth bhūmi, subdues all heterodox arguments up to and including those that are perverse and deluded, thereby taming all who practice evil paths. This refers to the passage in this very sutra concerning the establishment of great benefit (*mahārtha*), which refutes the doubts and attachments of outsiders; it is subsumed under the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) herein, because by abiding in the foundations of mindfulness, one overcomes what is perverse and deluded.

Furthermore, within this context, the purity of vision and knowledge (*darśana-jñāna-viśuddhi*) subsumes the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and so forth, thereby crushing heterodox arguments.

That sūtra further states: "The Tathāgata, in the sixth stage, establishes boundless sentient beings in the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the six great penetrations (*abhijñā*), namely: manifesting boundless buddha-fields adorned and purified by the merits of a buddha; manifesting being attended and surrounded by boundless bodhisattvas; manifesting buddha-fields that are vast and limitless; manifesting one's own body appearing within boundless buddha-fields; manifesting parinirvāṇa, up to the disappearance after preaching the Dharma; and manifesting boundless spiritual powers, supernormal knowledges, and transformations."

Those who possess the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are precisely those who have attained the divine eye, the mind of transformation, and the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna); since the foundations of mindfulness also encompass the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), and because this constitutes the practice of mastery over name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in both movement and stillness, one thereby leaves behind the obstacles to the supernormal powers and attains the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda).
Those six great powers arise solely from the Buddha; therefore, they are called "great.
Among these, the manifestation of the Buddha-land refers to the purification of this very realm.
The manifestation of Bodhisattvas attending upon him refers to the establishment of great Dharma benefits here, because by giving rise to hearing the Dharma, one immediately attends upon him.
Furthermore, because they do not abide in either nirvāṇa or saṃsāra, and are unstained by their activities for the benefit of living beings, there is the service [of attendants];
moreover, there is also service within the Pure Land, as its retinue and supporting assistants are all perfectly complete.
Manifesting the vastness of Buddha-lands is itself the perfection of purity.

Manifesting one’s own body within boundless lands refers to the nirvāṇa of non-abiding through these marks and signs; it is the manifestation of the body while flowing through saṃsāra without being defiled.
"Manifesting parinirvāṇa" means that all previous manifestations of the body have shown the appearance of extinction.

"Manifesting spiritual powers and supernormal faculties" refers to the mastery over the practice and abiding within the purification of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); because one has attained mastery through the contemplation of name-and-form, one transforms according to what is appropriate, giving rise to the application of supernormal faculties.

Furthermore, that sutra states: "The Tathāgata, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, truly reveals the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) on the seven stages, because they take the absence of intrinsic nature as their object of attachment. This is precisely what is meant here by "perfection of speech," wherein both the physical remains (śarīra) and the Dharma, as well as the teaching of the Dharma, are unstained.

Furthermore, it is said: "The Tathāgata, from the eighth stage onward, bestows the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon all bodhisattvas by means of four methods of answering. These four are described in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*: first, the prediction not made in one's presence; second, the prediction made in one's presence; third, the prediction based on the arousal of the mind; and fourth, the prediction based on the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This is precisely what is subsumed within the "perfection of speech" and so forth herein.

Furthermore, it says: "The Tathāgata, from the ninth stage onward, demonstrates [the path] to all bodhisattvas through skillful means. This refers generally to the manifestation of the three karmas (body, speech, and mind), which should be assigned accordingly according to their specific meanings.

Furthermore, it is said: "The Tathāgata, through the ten stages, teaches all bodhisattvas that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature; he utters the sound of Great Parinirvāṇa and speaks of the ultimate bliss of parinirvāṇa of all phenomena. This teaching can be understood according to its appropriate application.

However, that sutra primarily explains the ten stages of the Tathāgata based on the external benefits of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body); here, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and emanation-body are explained collectively. As for the correspondence between these meanings and the three bodies, it will be fully detailed below.
Question:

"Since this section below clarifies the merits of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), how does it compare—both in its similarities and differences—to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, and other such texts?"
Answer: "The great meaning may be the same, but they differ in their breadth and brevity.
The pure land where [the Buddha] resides, as described at the beginning of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, is precisely the pure land described here."
That sutra subsequently explains the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the essence of which is subsumed within what is here called the *dharmakāya*.

The third section of that sutra clarifies the essence of the Buddha’s four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*); this is not separate from what is here explained as being subsumed within the five eyes, the knowledge of others' minds, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and so forth.
This is because the categories of the four wisdoms also correspond accordingly to the five eyes and other such qualities.

However, those four wisdoms of the Dharma-realm in that Pure Land are all distinguished by multiple meanings; this clarifies the Buddha’s preaching through the form-body (*rūpakāya*), his perfect enlightenment regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), his non-abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, and his pure conduct and dwelling.

Although this [text] does not depart from the four wisdoms, it is not what is explicitly elucidated in that sūtra; therefore, it is explained here. Thus, there is a difference between this and that text in terms of elaboration and brevity.

Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, only this [point] should be judged. Judging the sūtra according to the śāstra, the text contains six sections, as has already been assigned to the sūtra above.

However, the aforementioned treatise states that the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains that there are six kinds of "endowment" (*paripūri*) which encompass the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

Regarding "endowment-encompassing transformation of the basis," this refers to the merits of the Tathāgata’s stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) among the six transformations of the basis; it specifically encompasses the fourth, the transformation of the basis as the perfection of fruition.

Among the four meanings of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), this refers to that which is attained through transformation, because it arises and is manifested according to whether it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Alternatively, although this explains the merits of the Buddha-stage, it is intended so that Bodhisattvas of the stages of Faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) and Purity (*śuddhi-bhūmi*) may—whether near or far—practice and seek them; thus they achieve the transformation of the basis. Among the six types of transformation of the basis, all five kinds are fully subsumed here, as appropriate to their respective stages.

Because the stages of practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita*), the pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*), and the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*) constitute the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), they do not include the inferior [stages]; yet the four meanings of the transformation of the basis also fully encompass these three stages, as they establish the four meanings from beginning to end.

Furthermore, among the four meanings of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the third—what is abandoned through transformation—is the total relinquishment of all inferior phenomena of birth and death, such as the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). Consequently, the Sūtra states: "One abandons the impermanent aggregates and attains the permanent aggregates."

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states that the transformation of the basis of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) occurs through the transformation of the basis of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Consequently, one attains mastery over the radiance of the physical body in the pure land, boundless sound, and the invisible crown of the head; it is within this mastery—specifically within the perfection of the two bodies characterized by the marks and signs of the pure land and their verbal expression—that "boundless sound" is found.

By means of the transformation of the basis of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), one attains the mastery of immeasurable, non-decaying great peace and bliss; this refers precisely to not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, and to the purity of conduct and dwelling.
By means of the transformation of the basis of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), one attains mastery in correctly teaching the collection of all names, phrases, and syllables;
this mastery of teaching is the perfection of speech, and it consists in the threefold understanding of names, phrases, and the meaning of the Dharma when bestowing the great benefit of the Dharma.

By transforming the basis of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), one attains the gathering of the Great Assembly and the attainment of mastery over pure phenomena; that is to say, when establishing the Dharma of great benefit, one gathers the great assembly and transforms the attainment of mastery over pure phenomena so that it enters their minds.

By means of the transformation of the basis of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one attains mastery over the wisdom of thorough discernment (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), and the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

"Thorough discernment" refers to the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*); the other three may be understood accordingly. These four wisdoms, in their respective order, constitute the essence of the Buddha’s eye, the wisdom-eye, and the dharma-eye, as well as the consciousnesses produced by the fleshly eye and the divine eye. Such is the coarse description; the ultimate principle should be further contemplated.
Because the four wisdoms extend to Buddhahood and are all the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).

Regarding the statement that the supports are fully encompassed: among the six fulfillments (*paripūri*), the fulfillment of transformation (*nairmāṇika-paripūri*) should be expanded to make seven; alternatively, within the six, the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) should be combined into the fulfillment of the body (*kāya-paripūri*) to constitute five fulfillments. However, the treatise excludes the extensive and adopts the concise, thus determining them as six.

Among the six [perfections], the first clarifies the perfection of the purity of the buddha-field; this is because it is an external fruit and serves as the vessel that supports [the internal qualities].

The scriptural passage consists of three parts: first, it clarifies that one who grasps at signs and adorns a self is not called a bodhisattva; second, it raises a question and provides an explanation regarding the intention to abandon the mind that grasps at signs and the adornment of a self; third, it formally exhorts entry into the principle of the two kinds of non-self through signless adornment.
The treatise consists of two parts: first, the indication of the purpose for which the sutra was brought forth; second, the formal explanation of the text.

Regarding the indication of the purpose, the phrase "for the sake of the *samāpatti* of the Pure Land" intends to reveal that the World-Honored One desires to cause Bodhisattvas to cultivate the causes of signlessness and realize the land of signlessness.

Regarding the "cause of signlessness," this refers to meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*); this passage exists because it is for the sake of causing Bodhisattvas to cultivate the causes of meditative equipoise in order to purify the Buddha-land.

Master Vasubandhu combines this section on the pure land with the preceding section on the elimination of pride into a single unit, as both serve to refute doubts. Thus, his treatise states: "Failing to penetrate the true Dharma-realm, yet giving rise to the intention to deliver sentient beings and to purify the Buddha-land—such a production of thought is itself a perversion. This demonstrates that if one has not realized *tathatā* (Suchness) and has not eliminated the two types of self-grasping, then giving rise to the intention to deliver sentient beings or the mind to adorn the land are both perversions; therefore, such a person is not a Bodhisattva.
The formal explanation of the text consists of two parts: first, the direct explanation of the scripture; second, a re-explanation of the previous "correct practice regarding the view of suffering.

Within the first part, there are three sections, corresponding respectively to the three segments of the scripture. In the third segment, the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*) are first explained.

Next, the repeated mention of "bodhisattva" within the scripture is explained to demonstrate the dual realization of the two selflessnesses; this is an interpretation based on the difference in wording. Alternatively, it may be interpreted as realizing only the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), for even those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are called "bodhisattvas."

Vasubandhu states: "Sentient beings and bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are without self; this is not through the self-cognition of faith of the non-saints, but through the wisdom of the saints. The meaning of this is as follows: ordinary sentient beings merely believe in and understand the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*), whereas the saintly bodhisattvas, by means of mundane and supramundane wisdom, realize and know the two kinds of selflessness. Thus, based on the distinction between ordinary beings and saints, the term "bodhisattva" is repeated. This is because the mundane and supramundane truths are each distinct. However, in the version by Kumārajīva alone, the repetition of "selflessness" is absent; alternatively, the single character "self" (*ātman*) may extend downward to both "self" and "phenomena" (*dharma*), while the mention of "bodhisattvas" is omitted due to abbreviation. Nevertheless, the meaning of the Pure Land is as explained elsewhere: the Buddha-body and its supporting land each have their own distinct characteristics.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: Furthermore, the self-nature body (*svabhāvakāya*) relies upon the dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*). Although there is no ontological distinction between this body and its land, they differ in terms of their attributes and nature as they belong to the Buddha’s qualities. The self-enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*) likewise relies upon its own self-enjoyment land; that is, the pure consciousness associated with the great perfect mirror wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), which, through the causes and conditions of the untainted practices for self-benefit cultivated in the past, achieves a purely immaculate Buddha-land. From the moment of initial enlightenment until the end of the future, it continuously transforms into a purely immaculate Buddha-land, circular and boundless, adorned with various jewels, upon which the self-enjoyment body constantly dwells.

The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) also resides in its own land; that is to say, through the power of the wisdom of equality and great compassion, and by virtue of the causes and conditions of the pure Buddha-land cultivated in the past for the sake of benefiting others, it manifests as a pure land according to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Whether small or large, inferior or superior, and changing from one state to another, the Enjoyment Body dwells in dependence upon it.

If the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) relies upon the transformation land, this refers to the wisdom of accomplishing activities (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna) through the power of great compassion. Due to the causes and conditions of the pure and impure Buddha-lands cultivated in the past for the sake of benefiting others, it manifests as a Buddha-land suited to the needs of bodhisattvas who have not yet reached the [bodhisattva] stages. Whether pure or impure, small or large, it undergoes successive transformations, and the Buddha’s transformation body dwells in reliance upon it.
Regarding the bodies and lands of the svabhāvakāya, because they are what all Tathāgatas equally realize, their essence is without distinction;
regarding the bodies and lands of the sāmbhogikakāya, although each Buddha’s is individually distinct, they are all boundless and do not obstruct one another;
as for the remaining two bodies and lands (the nairmāṇikakāya and the śuddhakāya), they are both common and uncommon to the sentient beings whom the various Tathāgatas transform.

In the preceding sutra, there was an exhortation to abandon the latter two and an exhortation to seek the former two, whereby one attains the two true adornments and is able to manifest the latter two. Therefore, what is explained here is similar in its application of the Dharma to the previous passage on "leaving behind minor objects of focus," though the intended audience differs.
In the preceding stage of the Ground of Practice through Faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*), both cause and fruit were not yet perfected;

however, because the Bodhisattvas of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) in the higher teaching achieve Buddhahood and a pure land through the fulfillment of their causes, they are accorded the name "Perfected" (*paripūrṇa*).

From here below is the second section, concerning the fulfillment of the purity of vision and knowledge (*darśana-jñāna-viśuddhi*). Among the six fulfillments, the preceding section clarified the external fruits, while this section reveals the internal fruits. Within the internal fruits, the purity of vision and knowledge is explained first because it is essential for the function of transformation; thus, there is this text to cause Bodhisattvas to seek it.
In the second section of the second part of Vasubandhu’s *Vyākhyā*, regarding the second doubt, it says: There is a doubt that asks:
"As previously stated, the Bodhisattva does not perceive others as sentient beings, does not perceive himself as a Bodhisattva, and does not perceive a pure Buddha-field; for what reason is this so?"
Because they do not perceive any phenomena, they are called "Buddhas. If this were the case, one might mistakenly think that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not perceive any phenomena at all.
It is to resolve this doubt that this passage is written.

Therefore, the intent of the treatise states: "Although one does not perceive all phenomena, it is not that there is no eye that cognizes objects; the five eyes of the Buddhas truly perceive those inversions. According to the commentary on the sūtra, this is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the purity of seeing and wisdom; second, clarifying the mastery of merit—namely, the two practices of merit and wisdom.

Regarding the first of the three sections [of the preceding], there is "vision" (darśana) at the beginning and "knowledge" (jñāna) at the end; this is because the five eyes and the knowledge of others' minds correspond respectively to these two.
The treatise is divided into two parts: first, the designation of names according to the sūtra; second, the formal explanation of the meaning.
In the explanation of the meaning, first comes wisdom (*jñāna*) and later merit (*puṇya*).

Within wisdom, first come insight (*darśana*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and subsequently the realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) within the wisdom of application (*prāyogika-jñāna*); thus, the following section provides a detailed analysis and clarification.

In the preceding section, the purity of vision was first elucidated. Within this discussion on the purity of vision, the initial part reveals the purpose of the scripture’s introduction, followed by the formal explanation of the five eyes.

The intent of the foregoing is as follows: because the Buddha has previously taught that all phenomena are empty, some may claim that the Buddha possesses only the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), or that only the wisdom-eye is supreme, or that he teaches only bodhisattvas to seek the Buddha’s wisdom-eye; it is for these reasons that the Buddha is said to possess the five eyes.
In order to demonstrate that the Buddha’s vision is pure and supreme, it is taught that there are five kinds of eyes, rather than only the single eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
As for how they are superior: the teaching of the first four eyes reveals their superiority among those within the realm of shared existence (*sabhāga-dhātu*);
the teaching of the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) reveals its superiority among all that is attained through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).

It is said that there is the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*); among the wisdom-eyes of the two vehicles and of bodhisattvas, the Buddha-eye is superior because it is uniquely possessed by the Buddha alone.
It is said that there is the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*); this demonstrates its superiority over all other fleshly eyes.
It is said that there is the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*); this demonstrates its superiority over all those attained through cultivation.
The mention of the "eye of wisdom" (prajñā-cakṣus) reveals its superiority over the eyes of wisdom of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas, for ordinary beings lack the eye of wisdom;
the mention of the "dharma-eye" (dharma-cakṣus) reveals its superiority among bodhisattvas, for those of the two vehicles lack the dharma-eye.
These four aforementioned types clarify that the Buddha’s vision surpasses what those [others] see; thus, they are equally superior.

It is said that there is the "Buddha-eye" to manifest that it belongs exclusively to the Buddha. Because the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) can perceive all phenomena not seen by others, it is called the purity of supreme vision.
If it were not stated that the Buddha possesses the five eyes, and the Bodhisattva-yāna were spoken before the Buddha, then one would seek only the Buddha’s wisdom-eye and not the other four;
in order to avoid this error, it is subsequently stated that the Buddha possesses the five eyes.
The general designation "eye" has the meaning of seeing objects;
because there are five ways of seeing objects, they are called the five eyes.

To explain the specific names: the four sensory objects are termed the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*); because this pure sense-faculty (*rūpa-indriya*) dwells in dependence upon flesh, it is called the fleshly eye.

Dhyāna is called "heaven" (deva); because one obtains the eye through heaven, it is named the "divine eye" (divyacakṣus). Wisdom (prajñā) indicates that which is able to see, while phenomena (dharma) indicate that which is seen. "Buddha" indicates the person; the meaning is thus to be understood.

The two eyes—the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) and the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*)—have pure matter derived from the four great elements as their nature. The physical eye is of the nature of being nurtured (*aupacayika*), transformed (*vaikṛta*), and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); the divine eye is said to be nurtured alone, based on its arising through cultivation that transcends obstructions.
The two eyes—the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and the dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*)—have wisdom as their nature;
the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) takes all four preceding types as its essence.
Nāgārjuna states that, for example, just as the four rivers flow into a great lake and are collectively termed the "great ocean," so too it is with the four eyes reaching the Buddha.

He further says: humans possess the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*); devas and others possess the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*); those of the two vehicles possess the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*); bodhisattvas possess the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*); and Buddhas possess the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*). It is on this basis that the five [eyes] are taught.

However, when the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is said to be called the "fruit of the Dharma," it is accomplished through the fulfillment of practice within the Buddha’s body; it is not a maturation of karma (*vipāka*). Therefore, because the Buddha’s five eyes are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas among other beings the fleshly and divine eyes (*divyacakṣus*) are exclusively tainted, their essential natures should be understood as explained in the treatise.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the three [eyes]—flesh, heavenly, and dharma—are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); however, the two eyes—the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and the Buddha eye (*buddha-cakṣus*)—also include the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). In their respective order:

the flesh eye sees what is near but not far, the coarse but not the subtle, the light but not the dark, and what is inside obstructions but not what is outside; thus, it is deficient in its function. Therefore, one cultivates the heavenly eye.

Although this lacks the aforementioned defects, it merely perceives the false appearances of forms and does not perceive the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; as it is not yet the path for transcending birth and death, one cultivates the wisdom eye.
Although one has attained the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), because there is still no knowledge regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), one cultivates the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*);
although one has attained the dharma-eye, because it is not yet exhaustive regarding all that is to be known, one cultivates the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*).

The sequence above has been explained in terms of one’s own practice; however, if the sequence is clarified in terms of transforming others, it is as follows: Having already perceived with the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) the various marks of suffering experienced by sentient beings—namely birth, old age, sickness, death, the affliction of greed, and mental distress—the Bodhisattva gives rise to compassion. Desiring to fully know the suffering and happiness of sentient beings within the six realms, he cultivates the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
Once the divine eye is attained, having seen the various torments such as being burned and boiled endured by sentient beings in the three evil paths, his compassion increases further.

Desiring to rescue and deliver them, he next cultivates the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). Although he has attained the wisdom eye, he does not yet know the methods for delivering sentient beings, nor does he yet know their faculties, inclinations, and dispositions; thus, there remains a deficiency in his ability to transform them, and so he cultivates the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).
Although one has attained the Dharma-eye, it is still inferior in terms of transforming others, as it is unable to universally transform all beings; therefore, one cultivates the Buddha-eye.
If one follows this treatise to distinguish the sequence, the explanation should be applied accordingly.

Regarding the two phrases concerning "that which is seen," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 14) states that there are three eyes: first, the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which can illuminate and perceive manifest forms without obstruction.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Among ordinary people, those with the most excellent fleshly eyes (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) do not surpass a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), who can see within a range of one hundred *yojanas*, yet only objects that lack luminous color;
if there are objects with luminous color, such as the sun, moon, or stars, even if they are at a great distance, other people are likewise able to see them.

The fleshly eyes (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) of the two vehicles are said to be the same as those of ordinary beings; however, the fleshly eyes of a bodhisattva, as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, are such that the inferior see a hundred *yojanas* and the superior see the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system.
Why is it not stated that one sees other directions? That treatise explains: because the Bodhisattva’s fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is still subject to obstructions, they cannot see other directions.

However, if one cultivates the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, then by means of the very fleshly eye born of one's parents, one will see the three thousandfold world system, reaching upward as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and will likewise perceive the good and evil causes and effects of sentient beings; this is similar to the aforementioned pure divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
This essence is the fruit of the Dharma; its function is the fruit of practicing the sūtras, not the fruit of practicing dhyāna.
Second, the divine eye can illuminate concealed and manifest, existent and non-existent obstructed forms.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Ordinary beings who cultivate and attain the divine eye see only one four-continent world (*cāturdvīpaka*). Lesser arhats see a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*); great arhats see a medium thousand-world system (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*); Aniruddha, through the power of his specialized cultivation, sees a great thousand-world system (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*); lesser pratyekabuddhas are the same as great arhats; and great pratyekabuddhas spontaneously see a great thousand-world system. These are all merely seeing the marks of the sense-object of form (*rūpa-dhātu*)."

The divine eye of a bodhisattva at its smallest range sees one hundred yojanas, up to the greatest bodhisattvas who see the boundless realms of the ten directions, being able to perceive forms that the various devas cannot see, as well as the causes and effects of the three periods of time.

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the divine eye of a śrāvaka perceives the false marks of forms (*rūpa*), but does not perceive the marks of their arising and ceasing, nor does it perceive the suchness (*tathatā*) of forms; thus, it differs from that of a bodhisattva.

When Śrāvakas perceive the characteristics of visual objects with their divine eye, they are the same as Bodhisattvas in that they do not perceive arising and ceasing; however, they differ from Bodhisattvas in other respects, though both are encompassed by the divine eye.

If that were so, Śrāvakas should possess the Dharma-eye, since their perception of objects is identical [to that of Bodhisattvas]; however, according to the *Mahā-śāstra*, when defining the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-eye, it is said to know the faculties, inclinations, and natures of sentient beings, as well as the various methods for delivering them—since Śrāvakas lack such wisdom entirely, they do not possess the Dharma-eye.

Third, the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is able to illuminate all modes of existence, whether material or immaterial; the essence of the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) is unified with wisdom as one. Unlike the physical eye, which is subject to destruction and possesses concealment or manifestation, it is therefore not discussed here in detail.
In this context, flesh and devas are combined because they are subsumed under "form" (rūpa);
whereas wisdom and phenomena are distinguished separately because one contemplates principle and phenomenon, and emptiness and existence are distinct.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* discusses only the causes [of vision], and thus speaks of only three types; this [text], however, asserts that the Buddha possesses them, and therefore includes all four or five eyes. Because he perceives all things spontaneously (*anābhoga*), he differs from the bodhisattvas.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) states that the Buddha-eye sees nothing it does not see, hears nothing it does not hear, and knows nothing it does not know; because these faculties function interchangeably, it is also able to hear and so forth.
The treatise correctly explains the five eyes, as the sūtra text contains five [sections], corresponding to the distinct nature of each of the five eyes.
In each instance, a previous Buddha first asks the question and Subhūti subsequently answers.

First, regarding the question "Do you possess the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*)?", since the sūtras state that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward there is no physical body, one might fear that the Buddha himself lacks the fleshly eye; therefore, this question and answer are necessary to demonstrate that the Buddha possesses the pure fleshly eye.

Because its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*), it surpasses all else; yet, with the exception of the Buddha, the vision of others by means of the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is not limitless. This [passage] contains three meanings—reliance, the description of characteristics, and aspiration—which cause the bodhisattvas to give rise to the mind of aspiration; therefore, these questions are posed. The subsequent sections should be understood accordingly.
In the *Nengduan* (The Capable of Severing), the text originally says "Tathāgata, etc. The inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) serves to cite the first title while implying the remaining nine.
Next, Subhūti’s response clarifies that those [nine] exist.

The Buddha asks according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) in order to manifest existence; thus, he answers according to convention by saying "it exists. All other cases should be understood accordingly.

Each instance cites what is seen by others to compare the Buddha’s superiority over the sensory range of ordinary people, as was already explained previously. As for the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), the two vehicles see only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) also attain a semblance of the wisdom-eye, while those on the ten stages truly attain it, yet because they still possess obscurations, they have not attained the state of a Buddha. Since this [Buddha-state] is the most supreme and manifest, he asks regarding it, and all other cases should be understood accordingly.
This treatise consists of two parts: first, the listing of the four or five eyes, categorized according to their expansion and contraction;
second, the [explanation of] the emptiness of objective realms.

Below, the meaning of the four eyes is explained. Within the explanation of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), only the sequence of its prior and subsequent stages is clarified, without listing or explaining individual definitions, as they can be readily understood.

From this point onward, within the section on "Wisdom and Purity," the scriptural text consists of three parts: first, it clarifies that the Tathāgata can know all various kinds of minds; second, it raises an inquiry and explains the reason for knowing many minds; third, it again raises an inquiry and explains the meaning of the non-abiding nature of the mind.
The preceding passage consists of six parts: first, the Buddha’s question;

second, Subhūti’s answer, in which he recognizes that the Buddha intends to use the sands of the Ganges as a numerical basis according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and thus replies by relying on conventional enumeration;
third, the repeated question; [and so forth].
4. A further response;
5. Revealing the multiplicity of sentient beings by means of the previously mentioned many realms;
6. Revealing the existence of multiple minds by means of the previously mentioned many births, because each birth involves many kinds of mind.
The treatise consists of two parts: first, the citation and application of scriptures; second, the formal explanation and resolution of difficulties.
Question:
"Why are the two eyes—the eye of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the Dharma-eye—not called 'knowledge' (*jñāna*)?"
If other mental states also perceive external objects, why are they not called "seeing"?
Why does the treatise speak of "cognition" (jñāna) [in this context]? Answer:
"The Dharma-gates are each distinct: if taken in the sense of illuminating objects, they are explained as the Gate of Vision;
if taken in the sense of decisive discernment, they are explained as the Gate of Wisdom. Question:

The *Mahā-śāstra* states that the Dharma-eye knows the faculties, inclinations, and dispositions of others; since this would also involve knowing the minds of others, why does this sutra separately mention the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) apart from the five eyes?
Answer: "In general, this refers to the Dharma-eye; the Buddha also knows the minds of others. However, the Buddha speaks of it now specifically because there is a distinct meaning [to be conveyed].

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Dharma-eye only knows the faculties, desires, and natures of sentient beings, and does not say that it knows the various types of minds of others, such as whether they possess greed or are free from greed."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* all state that the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) perceives whether another’s mind possesses greed or is free from greed, and so forth; they do not say it knows another’s faculties (indriya), inclinations (chanda), or nature (prakṛti).

According to these two texts, the *dharmacakṣus* (Dharma-eye) is specifically explained as not encompassing the minds of others. Although the *buddhacakṣus* (Buddha-eye) is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is attained as the Buddha-eye through the progression from the four eyes to the fruition; since the four [eyes] do not encompass the minds of others, the Buddha-eye is likewise the same.
Some claim that the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) also knows the minds of others; this is not so. If it did, how could it be called "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*)?
It is simply because the characteristics [of knowing other minds] are not manifest that, apart from the five eyes, the Buddha speaks of the knowledge of others' minds as a distinct faculty.

Furthermore, because the dharma-gates are each distinct, they are discussed with differentiation; however, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the three types of clear knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*) are likewise [comprised of] vision and wisdom.

Why, then, are the other powers and knowledges not mentioned? The power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi*) is merely a function of the body and does not possess the characteristics of wisdom or vision.

As for the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), although one hears sounds in order to know the minds of others, knowing those minds alone makes the hearing of sound non-essential; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Knowledge of past lives regarding future events is subsumed under the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and therefore is not mentioned here;

within the knowledge of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), that which takes one's own destruction of outflows as its object is subsumed under the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*), while that which takes the destruction of outflows in others as its object is known to be subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); for this reason, it is not mentioned.
Or it may be said that a single assembly is sufficient according to the needs of the audience; why must everything be complete?

In the formal commentary on the sūtra, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the mind’s abiding and its various modes; second, the interpretation that the mind’s abiding within the sūtra is itself non-abiding.

Regarding the term "abiding of the mind," the Tang edition reads "flowing and pouring" (*liuzhu*). This is because there is a fault in saying that the mind abides; upon investigating this mind, one finds it ultimately has no abiding place. Therefore, it is called "flowing and pouring," meaning that throughout the three periods of time, it flows and pours from moment to moment, with arising and ceasing in continuous succession, never departing from the three periods of time.

Regarding "several kinds," this refers to the aforementioned many lifetimes, clarifying that there are many types of minds among the classes of sentient beings; the meaning of this passage in the treatise is easy to understand.
The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that a bodhisattva’s knowledge of others' minds can know twenty-two types of minds among all sentient beings, such as those with greed and those without greed.

That treatise groups these meanings into eight categories: first, there are six types of mind—those accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as those free from greed, hatred, and delusion—which are termed "minds of secondary afflictions" (upakleśa-citta).
The seventh, the defiled mind, and the eighth, the non-defiled mind, are called "driving minds" (*sāsrava-citta*), referring to such minds as they correspond with other [mental factors].

The ninth, the limited mind; the tenth, the broad mind; the eleventh, the great mind; and the twelfth, the immeasurable mind—these four are called "arising minds," distinguished according to their mode of arising.

Those born in the four continents have limited knowledge and vision, and are thus called "limited minds. Those born in the six heavens of the desire realm have somewhat broader knowledge and vision, and are called "broad minds. Those born in the form realm have even greater knowledge and vision, and are called "great minds. Those born in the formless realm have immeasurable knowledge and vision, and are called "immeasurable minds."

Thirteenth is the concentrated mind; fourteenth is the unconcentrated mind. These are called the minds of one training in samādhi. One who trains in samādhi is said to have a concentrated mind; one who does not train in samādhi is said to have an unconcentrated mind.

The fifteenth is the concentrated mind and the sixteenth is the unconcentrated mind; these are called the minds that have attained samādhi. When one enters samādhi, it is called the concentrated mind; when one does not enter it, it is called the unconcentrated mind.
Seventeenth, the mind of liberation; eighteenth, the mind of non-liberation—these are termed the minds that are bound and those that are free from bonds.
Nineteenth, the seeking mind; twentieth, the non-seeking mind—these are termed the mind of deluded action; this is the mind that performs karma.
Twenty-one is the "superior mind" (*adhimātra-citta*) and twenty-two is the "unsurpassed mind" (*anuttara-citta*); these are termed the "mind of overweening pride" (*adhimāna-citta*).

Among these twenty-two minds, the four types—the small, the broad, the great, and the immeasurable—encompass both defiled and pure states; the remaining eighteen minds each consist of one defiled and one pure state.
These various states of mind cannot be described in detail; therefore, they are collectively referred to as "several kinds of mind.

Regarding the term "world" (*loka*) mentioned in the treatise, it refers to the temporal divisions such as the past and so forth, which comprise both the three periods of time across a single lifetime and the three periods of time within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

The various minds of defilement and purity arise and perish from moment to moment, never departing from the three periods of time; although these minds are numerous, the Tathāgata knows them all in their totality. Therefore, the Sūtra says that the Tathāgata knows them all.
Vasubandhu says: "What is inversion? The verse states:

'Various inverted consciousnesses, because they are separated from true mindfulness and do not abide in that true wisdom, are therefore called inversions. This refers to the four foundations of mindfulness; it means that while they are the [proper] abiding, [inverted consciousnesses] are non-abiding, and these four foundations of mindfulness are the inversions."

From here below is the second section, the explanation of "non-abiding," which has two parts: first, the presentation of the correspondence with the sūtra to establish the ultimate meaning; second, the explanation of the sūtra text regarding the statement that the minds of the three periods of time all lack substantial reality.
Regarding the phrase "For what reason," in the second passage, there is first an inquiry and subsequently an explanation.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* provides two explanations for this objection: first, since the Buddha’s mind always delights in emptiness and quiescence, how could he fully know the minds of all sentient beings?
2. How can the single mind of a Buddha know so many minds?
Therefore, it says, "For what reason?

The subsequent scriptural passage explains the reason for this knowledge: because the Buddha has realized all minds, they are said to be "not-mind"; and because he perceives the universal essence of all minds, he is able to know them all completely.
The *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā* states: "If one thoroughly knows the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, this is called 'omniscience' (*sarvajñatā*).
If one were to know them by traversing each phenomenon individually, even after a long period of time, one would be unable to know all phenomena."
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha also asks himself: "How does the Buddha know the defiled minds of sentient beings?
The Buddha explains that it is because the Buddha knows them by relying on the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: Although the minds of sentient beings are manifold, they do not deviate from the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; by relying on principle to illuminate phenomena, one is thus able to fully know all the various minds of sentient beings.

The "Mahāyāna Chapter" further states: If the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) of all sentient beings were substantially real and not illusory, the Buddha would be unable to know the various minds of all sentient beings.
Because the mental factors of sentient beings are illusory, having no place of origin and no place of departure, the Buddha is able to know the minds of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, it is said: if one discriminates and grasps at signs, one does not see the true nature of phenomena; because one does not see the true nature of phenomena, one cannot penetrate all things.

If one does not grasp at signs and the mind is free from discrimination, then one attains the true nature of phenomena; because one attains the true nature of phenomena, one is able to illuminate and know all phenomena.
The intent of this commentary is likewise: by stating that all mental abidings are in fact not mind, it is able to illuminate and know the various kinds of minds of sentient beings.

Next, the scriptural text is explained by inferring that the minds of the three periods of time all lack substantial reality. Among the various sūtras and śāstras, the present dharma is most often analyzed through the lens of momentary cessation (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), yet this does not entirely avoid dispute; for one might ask: if the characteristic of duration has not yet ceased, how could its existence be precluded?
Now, when we examine this through the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), even the characteristic of abiding for a single moment (*kṣaṇasthiti-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended.

From here on, the second section of the treatise provides a detailed analysis in two parts. First, regarding why "purity of vision" (*darśana-viśuddhi*) is mentioned first and "purity of knowledge" (*jñāna-viśuddhi*) is mentioned later, the treatise itself explains:

"Vision is established for the sake of realization within that which is to be known; knowledge is established for the sake of instructing various sentient beings to pacify their minds. Because one must first personally realize that which is to be known, "purity of vision" is mentioned first.

Having personally realized and understood [the truth], one next explains the knowledge of others in order to teach sentient beings to sever evil and cultivate good, which is termed the "mind of tranquility.
This constitutes the sequence of awakening oneself and then awakening others.

Next, because they are explained as being within the same dwelling place, the establishment of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) as neither mind nor non-mind within the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi*) is logically consistent; this is analogous to what was previously stated regarding the purity of vision (*darśana-viśuddhi*), where it was taught that the five eyes which can see are likewise neither eyes nor non-eyes. Thus, the principle is established.

If that is so, since the perfection of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*) and the perfection of vision and knowledge (*darśana-jñāna*) likewise abide in the same locus, why are they not established together following the passage on the perfection of merit? [The answer is: Merit is the cause of vision and knowledge; although they share the same locus, the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of merit and wisdom (*prajñā*) are different, and for this reason they are established separately.
From here below, the second is named "Endowment with Merit" (*puṇya-saṃpad*), which clarifies that the Buddha possesses the adornment of great merit and virtue (*mahā-puṇya*).

As for why it shares the same locus as vision (*darśana*) and knowledge (*jñāna*): this merit is the root of the aforementioned Buddha-knowledge; it is not inverted merit. Because he is adorned with such great merit and virtue, both vision and knowledge are purified, surpassing all others.

The *Treatise* by Maitreya Bodhisattva is the same; there, Maitreya himself provides a sub-section to refute the third doubt. The doubt states: "It was previously said that the mind abides in perversion (*viparyāsa*). If this is so, then merit (*puṇya*) is also perverted.
If it is perverted, how can it be called a wholesome dharma (*kuśala-dharma*)?"

To demonstrate that merit is not perverted, the verse says: "The root of the Buddha’s wisdom is non-perverted merit; because it possesses these characteristics of merit, further similes are spoken. From this point forward, all instances where merit is cited for comparison are causes of the Buddha’s wisdom, as they become increasingly superior through the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Alternatively, it may refer to cases where one personally undertakes only the superior merit of the supramundane, thereby measuring against oneself the merit of upholding and expounding [the teachings]; this differs from the aforementioned non-wisdom-based meritorious conduct.

The sūtra text consists of four parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the Buddha’s confirmation and elaboration, beginning with "If this heap of merit..."; and fourth, the refutation of attachment to names.

In Kumārajīva’s version, there is no introductory prose; furthermore, it separately places the section on the absence of merit (*puṇya*) below the main text. In that treatise, there are two parts: first, the heading of the title which belongs to the sūtra; second, the sequential explanation of the difficulties.

Regarding how one can perform the giving of the seven treasures filling the three thousandfold world system, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that an avaivartika bodhisattva is able to give away the seven treasures filling the three thousandfold world system.

Furthermore, the thirty-eighth [chapter] states: "A bodhisattva may offer the precious treasures of the three-thousandfold world system to the Triple Gem; subsequently, they may offer clothing, food and drink, kingdoms and cities, wives and children, head, eyes, body, flesh, and so forth, as well as the gift of Dharma and the gift of fearlessness, dedicating these with sympathetic joy. This extends even to the merit of filially supporting one's parents, making offerings to teachers and elders, and the virtues of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—all equal in measure to the Dharma-realm and the expanse of space."
For now, the question concerns filling the three thousandfold world-system with the seven treasures and making offerings to the two fields of compassion and respect.

If one says "if there were someone," this refers to those who cultivated meritorious deeds in the past; it is placed within the midst of difficult-to-understand matters because one fears that people might pursue the name of "merit" and give rise to attachment. Therefore, the ultimate meaning of merit is established to teach that while one should request the Bodhisattva to cultivate merit, one must not grasp at it, thereby avoiding the two faults of exaggeration and depreciation.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Because this accumulation of merit is with outflows (*sāsrava*), the Tathāgata does not call it an 'accumulation of merit'.
Another interpretation of its meaning is as follows: if the wholesome accumulation of merit belongs to the category of the Path (*mārgapakṣa*), then it is an accumulation of merit;

however, if the accumulation of merit does not belong to the category of the Path, the Tathāgata does not describe it as the root of wisdom. This is because there is a distinction between the category of merit (*puṇyapakṣa*) and the category of the Path, or between that which is with outflows and that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*). Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of the "accumulation of merit" twice.

The third major section below concerns the treatise titled "The Endowment of the Body with the Minor Marks (Anuvyañjana) and the Major Marks (Lakṣaṇa). This passage clarifies that the Buddha transforms the basis of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), thereby attaining the physical body endowed with the marks and minor marks of the Buddha-ground. It thus causes Bodhisattvas to seek the eighty minor marks. As explained in various sutras such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the *Nirvāṇa*, there is the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, this appears at the beginning of the eighty minor marks, while in the *Nirvāṇa*, it appears at the end of the thirty-two major marks.

If one consults the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Dharaṇīśvara-paripṛcchā-sūtra* to compare and evaluate the merits of the marks and signs, the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdha*) is the greatest; nevertheless, in various sūtras, it appears at the beginning of the list of the eighty secondary marks (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*).
The structure of the sutra—question first and answer later—is clear from the treatise’s analysis.

This question contains two intentions: first, it asks according to the meaning of "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*), which aims to shatter the Bodhisattva’s grasping at the signs of the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) and cause them to seek [the Buddha] with a signless mind;

second, it asks according to the intention of "explaining characteristics," which reveals that the Buddha’s body is fully endowed with the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*) in order to inspire the Bodhisattva to give rise to a mind of aspiration and longing.

Regarding the statement, "The Tathāgata speaks of the perfection of the physical body, yet it is not a perfection of the physical body," this is an interpretation based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Since the Buddha, in various passages of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, explains that the eighty minor marks are empty, he says that what the Tathāgata speaks of is "not" [that very thing].

If that is so, why is it necessary to analyze these eighty minor marks? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explains that there are eighty kinds of celestial beings among the worldly sentient beings; each of those eighty deities possesses one of the minor marks, which inspires people to have faith and incline toward them. In order to transform those sentient beings who worship such deities so that they may enter the Buddha-dharma, and to cause those deities to abandon their arrogance, the Buddha manifests all eighty marks upon a single body. It is for the sake of seeking [the truth] that he raises this question.
Because Subhūti’s question was intended to dismantle attachment, he established the form-body (*rūpakāya*) as the ultimate truth; therefore, he stated that it is "not indeed a complete form-body.

As for the statement, "Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'complete form-body,'" this is said in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) to fulfill the bodhisattva’s aspiration for the Buddha’s form-body.

The fourth treatise, titled "The Endowment of the Body of Names and Characteristics," shares a similar structure with the "Excellence of the Conforming Characteristics"; both may be understood by following the explanations provided previously for the subsequent sections.

In Vasubandhu’s treatise, the third major section from here on down refutes doubts. Specifically, the two preceding doubts arise from the fundamental tenets of the school itself, while the four subsequent doubts all arise through successive progression.
Within this passage there are three sections; this is the first.
It addresses a doubt that might arise:

"If the Buddhas are designated by the name 'Buddha' because of their unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), how is it that they are called Buddhas for accomplishing the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two major marks?"
Because the physical characteristics and features of the Master Asaṅga were distinct, [the text] is divided into two sections;
whereas because the Bodhisattva Master Vasubandhu shared the same doubt regarding the destruction of the material body, they are combined into one.
That treatise states: "The ultimate essence of the Dharma-body is not that body of marks and signs, because it is not accomplished through marks, nor is it that [conventional] Dharma-body.

Yet, being inseparable from the Dharma-body, those two are not non-Buddha; therefore, 'accomplishment' is spoken of again, and there is neither duality nor self. This is because such things do not exist within that Dharma-body, it is said that they are "not accomplished";
yet because they are not separate from that Dharma-body, it is said that they are "accomplished."
The remaining words are easy to understand.
From here below is the fifth discourse, titled "Awakening to Fulfillment," which reveals that the fulfillment spoken of by the Buddha’s verbal activity is the subject to be explained.
If this is so, how does it reveal the fulfillment of what the Buddha has spoken?

This means that just as the physical body with its marks and signs was described previously, it can manifest those marks, signs, and exquisite colors even within the formless realm; likewise, the Buddha’s speech is such that it can fully expound the Dharma even within the state of non-explanation. Therefore, the treatise names this "perfection of speech."

However, within the stage of Buddhahood, the merits of the Tathāgata’s three types of action are revealed in general. Since it is stated that "vision and wisdom are pure," this reveals the merit of the Tathāgata’s mental action;
since it is stated that "the form-body is perfected," this reveals the merit of his physical action;
and since it is stated that "speech is perfected," this reveals the merit of his verbal action.
Regarding "the perfection of mind," this reveals the manifold functions performed by the Tathāgata’s mind, which will be clarified below.
In the second sub-section of Vasubandhu’s commentary, a doubt arises:
"Since the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and its marks (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended, how does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma?"

To sever this doubt, the verse states: "As with the Buddha, so it is with the Dharma; the two attachments mentioned are distinct, yet they do not depart from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), for the teaching of the Dharma has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva). This means that both the teaching and its meaning, as explained, cannot be found to possess an intrinsic nature apart from the true dharma-realm; this is consistent with the present treatise.

The sūtra text consists of four parts: first, the question; second, the refutation; third, the inquiry into and explanation of the reason for that refutation; and fourth, the further inquiry into and explanation of the reasons why [the interlocutor] does not understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught.

There are two types of treatises, which may be understood by analogy with what precedes; here, however, it merely states that "there is no dharma that can be taught" without explaining the reason why.
The eight-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states that the non-teaching of dharmas is based on two meanings.

First, based on the Dharma realized within my own inner realization, which is free from the marks of verbal discrimination and free from the marks of names and words, I do not see a single dharma that can be spoken.

Second, based on the path of the ancient sages, I now speak solely by relying on the old path of the Buddhas of antiquity; this path has existed eternally, just as when one proceeds toward the attainment of the Way. Outside of the old path of the Buddhas of antiquity, there is not a single word that can be spoken; therefore, it is said that "there is no dharma that can be spoken," and this is called "preaching the Dharma."
Regarding the two aspects of dharma and meaning, the term "dharma" is repeated; however, according to Kumārajīva’s version, this repetition is absent.

From here on, the sixth section is titled "The Fulfillment of Mind. This section clarifies the six types of mental functions of the Buddha, culminating in the sixth point which clarifies the purity of the Buddha’s three karmas in walking and staying. Since walking and staying through body and speech are also the operations of the Buddha’s mind, the treatise is collectively titled "Fulfillment of Mind."

The preceding treatise analyzes this passage as having six further divisions, as previously assigned. Herein, the first clarifies the merit of the Buddha’s three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); thus, it is called "foundations of mindfulness.
Vasubandhu’s third son raised a doubt, asking:

"If one says that what the Buddhas speak is the teaching of non-dharma and is not separate from the *dharmakāya*, then who is there capable of believing such profound and subtle meanings of the Dharma?"
The scriptural text consists of two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.

Within the answer, there are two sections: first, an initial response based on the two truths, utilizing both the contemplations of emptiness and existence; second, a further inquiry and explanation to establish the meaning.

This treatise consists of three parts: first, the designation of its affiliation with the Sūtra; second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; and third, the commentary on the Sūtra text. Regarding the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion, it states:

"Because this section demonstrates that [the Buddha] causes [beings] to abide as the World-Honored One does; herein it clarifies that toward those who believe and those who slander, the Buddha is in every way like the World-Honored One, maintaining a single impartial mindfulness. Since this is explained in reference to three types of persons, it is called the 'Three Stations of Mindfulness' (trayo manasikārāḥ)."

"Are there perhaps those in the future who will develop faith? Here, one who trusts the Buddha’s words is cited; alternatively, one who does not trust them is cited. These two—faith and slander—are objects that stir the mind; therefore, they are singled out, while those who are neutral are not. This is because favorable and adverse conditions exist at all times and in all places.
Now, for the time being, in order to explain the purpose of this treatise based on what has been heard from this sutra, I shall interpret Subhūti’s question in the sutra.

There are two parts to this interpretation: first, the explanation of the Buddha’s reply; second, the explanation of the Buddha’s intent regarding those who would believe in the Dharma. If one contemplates the nature and characteristics of sentient beings through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and finds them both empty, saying that they are not "sentient beings," this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
If there were absolutely no sentient beings, from where would the Buddha give rise to the thought of equality?
According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is not that provisional sentient beings do not exist; this is the contemplation of the provisional.

Since there are no real objects of either opposition or compliance within emptiness or conventional designation, the Buddha gives rise to a single thought of equality toward those who believe and those who slander him.
Next, he provides a further inquiry and explanation to establish the preceding meaning.
The *Anāsravabhāṣya* does not provide an explanation because it is easily understood.
Its underlying intention is as follows: since it has already been stated that they are not sentient beings (*sattva*), why does it further say "not"?

The phrase "sentient beings, sentient beings" reiterates the two explanations of emptiness and conventionality; "not sentient beings" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); and "these are called sentient beings" relies upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Furthermore, the subsequent discussion in the treatise explaining those who have faith in the Buddha and the Dharma states that such persons are "the most rare of all"; this demonstrates the teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is both unique and harmonious.

The meaning of this interpretation is as follows: if one wishes to believe that the Buddha’s words can benefit people, yet believes that what the Buddha said regarding them is that they are not sentient beings, this reveals the "unshared" (asādhāraṇa) meaning by way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If one believes that what was said is not that they are not sentient beings, this reveals the "corresponding" (anuloma) meaning by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Because such a person is difficult to encounter, it is called "supremely rare."
The original texts all lack these passages; however, although the Buddha is impartial toward both faith and slander, the present mention of "faith" does not imply a lack of impartiality.

Vasubandhu’s *Śāstra* states: "That which is taught and the teacher are profound; it is not that there are none capable of faith; they are neither sentient beings nor non-sentient beings, neither noble ones nor non-noble ones. The first two lines directly answer the preceding doubt, while the latter two lines explain the response of the Tathāgata to Subhūti’s question. This demonstrates that those capable of faith in this sutra are not ordinary sentient beings; therefore, it says they are "not sentient beings," yet because they are noble sentient beings, it says they are "not non-sentient beings."
This passage is missing from the version by Kumārajīva;

it constitutes the second section within the "Perfection of the Lower Mind. The treatise here is titled "Perfect Enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*), and this section clarifies the meaning of the Buddha’s attainment of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
In Vasubandhu’s treatise, from this point forward begins the fourth major section, "Refuting Doubts. This section consists of three parts; this is the first.
The doubt is as follows:

"If the Tathāgata does not attain even a single dharma called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how is it that, through successive stages of higher and higher realization, he progressively attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

This doubt arises either regarding the passage stating that the Tathāgata previously, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, "actually obtained nothing at all" concerning the Dharma, or it arises regarding the passage concerning the prediction (vyākaraṇa) bestowed by Dīpaṃkara.

Since not a single dharma can be apprehended, this is precisely the realization of the Dharma that is detached from its superior nature. How, then, can it be said again that one progressively attains unsurpassed bodhi?
The scriptural passage consists of three parts: first, the question; second, the answer; and third, the confirmation and restatement.
In Kumārajīva’s version, the text of the response is missing.
The treatise consists of two parts: first, the designation of the title and its connection to the sūtra;
second, the formal exposition. Within the exposition, there are three sections: first, the explanation of the words of the response; second, the interpretation of the seal and the narrative.

Although this is not explained in detail, within the question there are three intended meanings: the meaning of the basis (*artha*), the meaning of the characteristics of the teaching (*lakṣaṇa*), and the meaning of the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
Regarding the meaning of the basis: this question is intended to refute the Bodhisattva’s attachment to the notion of attaining unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Regarding the Buddha’s question concerning the intention behind the second explanation of the characteristics: this question is intended to explain the characteristics of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
As for the "intention of aspiration," it is to cause all Bodhisattvas to give rise to a mind of aspiration and resolve toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddha.
Subhūti replied: "It is also because one establishes the Buddha’s unsurpassed enlightenment as the ultimate truth that he first answered directly, 'No,' and then said, 'World-Honored One!'"
Regarding the phrase "there is no dharma [attained by] the Tathāgata," this explains the meaning of the word "not" (*na*).
Thus, the Commentary states: "There is no dharma" is said in order to eliminate the view of existence; it teaches that the Buddha did not attain even the slightest dharma as bodhi.
This not only reveals that the Buddha is free from the view of existence, but also causes those on the stage of the purified mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*) to abandon the view of existence.

If one asks, "If there is absolutely no attainment, why does this not fall into the error of the view of non-existence?"—if there were truly neither view nor attainment, that too would indeed be an error; however, because the illness of the view of existence arises most frequently, this is stated as a specific countermeasure. This is because the Buddha has transcended both views of existence and non-existence.
In the "Explanation of the Seal" (*mudrā-vyākhyāna*), the sūtra text first presents the seal and subsequently provides the commentary.
The section beginning with "I, regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...

constitutes the commentary. As the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu states in his treatise: "In that place there is not even the slightest dharma; one knows that awakening is unsurpassed. The *dharmadhātu* neither increases nor decreases; it is the pure, equal intrinsic nature."
"There is the unsurpassed skillful means, and it is free from the phenomena of outflows; therefore, that which is not a pure phenomenon is itself the pure phenomenon.

He explains the meaning of "unsurpassed" regarding the Buddha’s bodhi through four points. First, he clarifies that within the Buddha’s bodhi there is not a single further dharma to be obtained; thus one knows that bodhi receives the name "unsurpassed. This corresponds to the first two lines [of the verse], as can be understood from the sutra.

Second, from "This Dharma is equal" onwards, it clarifies that the Buddha realizes the equal *dharmadhātu* without increase or decrease; because there is nothing superior to it, it is called "unsurpassed," which corresponds to the third phrase.

Third, from "because there are no sentient beings" onwards, it clarifies that the Buddha’s Dharma-body is equal and without differentiation; furthermore, because the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is the true essence and is unsurpassed among all things, it is called "unsurpassed," which constitutes the fourth phrase.

Below the phrase "all wholesome dharmas," it is clarified that the Buddha’s bodhi possesses unsurpassed skillful means for cultivating all roots of goodness; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed. This is designated as "unsurpassed" in contrast to the two vehicles.

This second section of the treatise, which provides an exegesis and commentary on the scriptural seal, contains two parts: namely, *bodhi* (enlightenment) and the path to *bodhi*. First, by way of the fruit, it clarifies that the Buddha’s *bodhi* possesses the sense of being unsurpassed; this is the *bodhi* indicated at the outset.

Second, from the phrase "all wholesome dharmas" (*sarvakuśaladharmāḥ*) onwards, it explains through the perspective of the cause how the Buddha’s *bodhi* possesses the sense of being unsurpassed awakening; this is the path to *bodhi* indicated at the outset.

The preceding section has two parts, namely, because there are two distinct statements; these two statements correspond to and explain the Dharma-body and the Reward-body, as should be understood according to their meaning.
The treatise itself has two parts: first, the presentation of the two types, and second, the corresponding explanation.
In the initial passage, the preceding section first restates and assigns [the terms], because this reveals the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of bodhi.

The subsequent section explains the meaning; within that explanation, the phrase "because it is the intrinsic characteristic of bodhi" clarifies that when a Buddha attains bodhi, although he realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, he does not perceive through discrimination that there is an attainment. This interprets the scriptural statement that "bodhi is unattainable," because its intrinsic characteristic cannot be attained.

Regarding the phrase "because it has the characteristic of liberation": one does not perceive a substantial entity of bodhi; this explains that such a thing cannot exist, because the characteristic and essence of liberation—which is the state of being free from obstructions—are unattainable.
The section below that [passage] provides a further explanation of the conclusion.

Both the versions by Kumārajīva and Weijing state collectively that "there is not even the slightest dharma to be obtained. The Tang version and the Paramārtha version both place "non-existence" first and "non-attainment" last. If this is the case, then "non-existence" is explained through the self-characteristic of bodhi, because one does not see the self-substance of bodhi as existing; "non-attainment" is explained through the characteristic of liberation, because one does not see liberation as something that can be attained.

Some explain it as follows: "There is no [knower]" means that although one has attained the wisdom of supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi-jñāna*), one does not perceive a self that is capable of awakening;

"there is no attainment" means that although one has attained the true nature (*dharmatā*) of what is attained, one also does not perceive a true nature that is attained. This should be understood according to the discourse, which corresponds to what is taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: "there is neither knowing nor attaining."

The intended meaning of this explanation is as follows: within the first statement, both the means of realization (*pramāṇa*) and the object realized (*prameya*) are included; within the second statement, it refers exclusively to the wisdom that realizes.

According to the original True Dharma, the initial phrase—"there is no dharma that the Tathāgata abandons"—clarifies the Buddha’s transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); when abandoning the obstacles to be eliminated, he does not perceive even the slightest dharma to be abandoned, which reveals the characteristic of Bodhi and liberation.

The subsequent phrase—"there is no dharma that the Tathāgata attains"—clarifies the Buddha’s attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment; regarding all dharmas, he attains unimpeded knowledge and vision, yet he perceives neither the subject that attains nor the object attained. This reveals the characteristic of the Buddha’s unsurpassed enlightenment, and is therefore called the "intrinsic characteristic of Bodhi."

The second section below explains the term "Buddha. The title of the Sūtra is *Bodhi* because it encompasses both the Two Vehicles and the relationship between cause and effect; therefore, the title of the Śāstra is *Buddha*, as it refers exclusively to the fruit of Buddhahood.
