Answer: "Because ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles cannot break down atoms, they either cling to atoms as being real and permanent, or they cling to the notion that there are real atoms within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). To refute such false attachments, it is said: 'If a collection of atoms existed in the ultimate truth, the Buddha would not have called them a multitude of atoms.'"

Furthermore, the fourth layer of inquiry asks: Why did you previously state that if atoms existed in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the Buddha would not have spoken of them as a "multitude of atoms"?

Next, the fifth section below cites what was previously said before the Buddha; it accords with the Buddha’s prior statement that atoms are not atoms. Thus, we know that the question regarding whether they are many was intended to further reveal that they are not atoms.

Therefore, the treatise states: "The World-Honored One said that a collection of atoms is not a collection; it is called a 'collection of atoms' because the substance of this collection is not established."
If it were otherwise, even without being stated, one would naturally know this to be an aggregate; for what purpose, then, would it need to be stated?

When the Buddha asks whether the particles are many, he clarifies that the substance of the subtle particles (*paramāṇu*) is empty. If this were not the case, and the body of form were merely broken down into many particles, then both ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles would already know for themselves that these are many particles; why then would it be necessary to ask whether the particles are many?
Thus, one should know that this question is a skillful means for demonstrating that nothing is perceived.

Having thus employed two types of skillful means to refute the physical body, it has been conclusively clarified that the objective portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) is without anything to be grasped and is non-existent.

Next, the following section refutes the notion that the "name-body" (nāmakāya) is not non-existent; this can be understood from the sutra text. The treatise contains two parts: first, it cites the sutra and assigns its meaning, pointing out that it is identical to what was previously explained;
second, it clarifies that the world belongs exclusively to sentient beings, which are merely name-bodies.
Now, observing that the realm of the body of names (*nāmakāya*) is empty, it is said that the world is "not [a world].

From here below begins the second major section, which combines the refutation of the body of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). By means of both the subject and object of grasping, it is shown to be signless (*animitta*) and unarisen (*anutpāda*); because it refutes the grasping mind so that it does not arise, it is called "unarisen."
The passage contains three parts: first, a re-examination based on the preceding;
second, from "If the world... onwards, pointing out the substance of the attachment;
and third, from "The Tathāgata says... onwards, the actual refutation.

Now, as for the phrase "for what reason," this raises a challenge based on what preceded: for what reason was it previously stated that atoms are not actually atoms and that worlds are not actually worlds?

The second subsequent explanation also points out the substance of the attachment, stating: "If one clings to atoms, name-bodies (*nāmakāya*), or realms (*dhātu*) as being substantially existent, these are all merely the 'unified' delusion within conceptual construction."
Therefore, the commentary states: "Within this, both the world and the realm of atoms are described together; these two are both merely false imaginings of a unified whole (*saṃghāta-vikalpa*).

Why is the unified characteristic of the physical body (*rūpakāya*) not also cited? It is because the characteristics of the physical body are coarse and easily understood, whereas the characteristics of the realms and atoms are subtle and difficult to understand; therefore, they are specifically refuted."
If one clings to these two as being substantially existent, this is the deluded conception of a "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍa-vikalpa*), not the [delusion of] signs or letters.

Therefore, the new edition calls it the "clinging to a unified whole," while the Paramārtha edition calls it the "clinging to an accumulation. This is precisely the "clinging to a part" (*ekadeśa-grāha*) within the eight types of discrimination in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, and it is also the "accumulation delusion" (*saṃcaya-vikalpa*) among the eight delusions in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Regarding the eight types of conceptualization: first, conceptualization of conjunction is greed; second, conceptualization of non-conjunction is anger; third, conceptualization of both conjunction and non-conjunction, as well as their opposites, is delusion. These three constitute those afflictions.
Fourth, the false imagination of "I," which refers to clinging to oneself as a self;
fifth, the false imagination of "mine," which refers to clinging to sentient beings as belonging to oneself—these two are the afflictions of the flesh.
Sixth, the delusion of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), which refers to clinging to all phenomena as having an intrinsic nature; it is also called the discrimination of intrinsic nature.

Seventh, the delusion of differentiation (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*), which refers to clinging to phenomena as having differentiations such as large and small, good and bad; it is also called the discrimination of differentiation.
Eighth, the delusion of accumulation (*saṃghāta-vikalpa*), which arises from grasping at a single entity within a combination of many things; these three are afflictions of the mind.

Subhūti understands that the collection of name-bodies (*nāmakāya*) and the collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*) are both composites formed from many things; although he previously refuted them as being non-existent by breaking them apart, he fears that beginners might still give rise to a grasping at unity. Therefore, he reiterates: if one grasps the realm of name-bodies and the realm of atoms as being substantially real, these are both instances of a "composite mark" (*ekasaṃyogalakṣaṇa*).
The treatise speaks of two kinds of grasping: namely, grasping as a whole (*piṇḍa-graha*) and grasping by differentiation (*prabhedataḥ piṇḍa-graha*).

"Whole" refers to a unified mass, while "grasping" refers to the apprehension of characteristics. However, since the world is a collection of named entities (*nāmakāya-dhātu*) that cannot be broken down from one into many, it constitutes grasping as a whole.
Because atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the differentiated components within the aggregate of form (*rūpakāya*), those who grasp at the existence of atoms constitute grasping by differentiation.

The treatise states that because one grasps at the accumulation of subtle atoms, Subhūti speaks in order to shatter these two attachments; he first points out that both of these attachments are, among the eight types of false conceptualization, the "conceptualization of a unified whole."
The third [section] cites what was previously stated before the Buddha in order to directly refute the notion of a "unified whole" (*piṇḍagrāha*).

The treatise states: "That which is not a grasping of a mass is called the establishment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)," meaning that the establishment of the unified whole is designated as the ultimate truth.
Regarding the phrase "this is called a unified whole," it is provisionally designated as a "unified whole" based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
From here on, the third major section consists of the Tathāgata’s confirmation of Subhūti’s explanation; logically, this should also include the separate refutation of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*).
Because the subsequent phrase "the breaking of name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is combined [with the preceding], it is established through specific exposition.

The intent of the subsequent passage is as follows: from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), that grasping (*piṇḍa-graha*) exists; however, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), that dharma is inexpressible. Thus, it is said that within the ultimate truth, no such grasping can be expressed. Yet, ordinary worldlings (*bāla*) and those of the two vehicles do not understand that the "unified appearance" (*eka-piṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) is empty; they merely pursue names and cling to them with force. Therefore, the treatise cites a sūtra, saying: "Those childish worldlings grasp according to verbal expression; this is not the ultimate truth."
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Ordinary beings grasp [reality] erroneously by merely following sounds. This is the explanation of the present passage.

From here on, the second major section of the text clarifies that there is no conceptual discrimination when performing the two contemplations; this teaches that one should not engage in discrimination when entering the samādhi of correspondence.

Regarding this, the first vehicle first raises an objection: "If a unified appearance is not itself a perception of unity, but is merely that which ordinary people grasp through attachment, then views such as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and other views should likewise not be considered 'views. For what reason, then, does the Buddha say that ordinary people possess the view of self, the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and so forth?"
This treatise cites the sūtra; furthermore, neither Kumārajīva’s version nor the present text contains corroborating passages for this.

Second, the refutation of the attachment to views such as the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) consists of three parts within the text: first, the question; second, the answer; and third, the Buddha’s confirmation and fulfillment of the point, which also serves as an exhortation to bodhisattvas that all phenomena should be known, seen, and understood in this manner.

The treatise consists of two parts: first, the explanation of the preparatory methods for meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); second, the revelation of the reasons why the methods for desire, aspiration, and the gathering of the distracted are not mentioned.

Within the first part, there are three sections: first, concluding what has already been explained and indicating what remains unsaid; second, setting forth questions regarding four gates; third, providing detailed explanations according to those headings.

The preceding general and specific refutations of the notions of "non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñā*) and "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) are, taken together, all skillful means (*upāya*) of the school that maintains there is nothing to be seen; therefore, it is said they have already been explained. What has not yet been explained is the samādhi associated with the realization of the ultimate and conventional truths by one whose mind is purified, because such a person does not engage in conceptual discrimination.
Next, regarding the explanation of the correlations, first this specific passage is correlated and explained, followed by applying the same principle to the remaining dwelling places (*vihāra*).
Within the former, the initial question and answer demonstrate "that which is not conceptually differentiated" (*avikalpita*);
the phrase "the bodhisattva who has generated the resolve" demonstrates "which person does not differentiate."
Regarding "all phenomena," this indicates which phenomena are not to be conceptually differentiated.

As for the fourth [point], what is the skillful means that贯通 (interpenetrates) the preceding question-and-answer and the subsequent contemplation? Knowledge, vision, and resolute belief are all skillful means of non-differentiation; therefore, having explained the question-and-answer, it says: "Contemplating the bodhisattva in this way... even this very observation is the skillful means for entry."

In the third major section of this work, Vasubandhu clarifies that the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) lack substantial reality. As the verse states: "One does not attain the Way through non-duality, for one must be far removed from [the views of] self and phenomena. This means that enlightenment is not attained by denying the existence of these two—the self and phenomena; rather, it is only by relinquishing these two views that one attains enlightenment. Thus, this verse provides a general explanation of the intent of the entire treatise.

Regarding the initial explanation in Asaṅga’s commentary on how there is no conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*): first, the inquiry is raised and the response indicated; second, the sūtra text itself is correctly explained.

Within the explanation of the sūtra text, there are three parts: first, the citation of the sūtra and its classification; second, the correct explanation through question and answer; and third, from "observing in this way" onwards, the conclusion that integrates the skillful means, because these same questions and answers are applied universally to whatever skillful means may be used.

Within the section on the correct resolution of questions and answers, first, the intent of the question is as follows: How is it demonstrated that one does not engage in conceptualization in accordance with what is not conceptualized?

Granted that although the Buddha taught that ordinary beings possess views of a self, a person, and so forth, one should know that the essence of these views is empty; thus, one should not give rise to the conceptualization of grasping at existence in accordance with what the Buddha taught. If this is so, for what reason did the Buddha say that ordinary beings possess views of a self, a person, and so forth?
The Commentary states: "What the non-Buddhists call the 'self,' the Tathāgata calls the 'view of self'; therefore, he establishes the selflessness of persons. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"As the ignorant discriminate, external objects do not truly exist at all; it is because the mind is agitated and turbid by habitual tendencies that it manifests as if those objects were present."

Because the Buddha taught the existence of a self (*ātman*) in order to refute the views of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), he stated that ordinary worldlings merely possess the false view of clinging to a self, whereas in reality no such self exists. As the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "In order to eliminate the real self and dharmas clung to by foolish worldlings, one conventionally designates the names 'self' and 'dharma' with respect to what is transformed by consciousness."

Now, it is revealed that the Buddha’s teaching shows that the grasped self (*ātman*) does not exist; rather, because he speaks of that "view of self" as being merely conventional, it is identical in meaning to that [previous] point.

When the Buddha says that ordinary beings possess the view of self, this is intended only to establish the principle of the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*). However, when internal ordinary beings (*ābhyantarapṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles hear the Buddha say that ordinary beings possess the views of self and person, they further grasp at the Buddha’s statement that there is a view of self and person; this constitutes attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*).

Now, within this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the Buddha comprehensively refutes the views and conceptual discriminations of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, and reveals that the essence of all such views is empty; therefore, he questions Subhūti.

The commentary explains the intent of this question as follows: The Buddha spoke of the existence of the view of self for the sake of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles; desiring to clarify that the essence of the view of self is empty and to reveal the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), he therefore posed this question.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "In order to enter into the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), the six pairs of dharmas are taught.
Furthermore, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "By relying on this teaching, one can enter into the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*);
as for the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) regarding the objects grasped by conceptualization, one enters it by relying on other teachings."
All such passages are explained in this same manner.
The response consists of three parts: first, a direct answer; second, a counter-interrogation; and third, an explanation by citing the Buddha’s own words.

Since the Buddha previously stated within the "Establishment of Great Benefit" that the notion of a self is itself not a characteristic of a self, those who maintain that the Buddha taught the view of a self do not speak correctly.

Why does the Buddha say that the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth are not actually views? The treatise states: "If there is such a view of self, it is subsumed under [false] views. This means that if one clings to a view of self, it is still subsumed under the view of clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha-dṛṣṭi*), as it obstructs entry into the corresponding samādhi; therefore, the Buddha taught that the view of self and so forth are not truly views.

Therefore, Vasubandhu’s treatise states: "To see the self is to not see it; there is no reality, for it is a false vision. This is a subtle obstruction; by seeing true suchness, one is free from it. This reveals that the view which clings to a self fundamentally does not see a self, because it lacks substantial reality and is merely a false vision; thus, the view of self has no essence.

The same applies to the view of phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*): when one realizes suchness (*tathatā*), one does not perceive the two types of self; thus, these subtle obstacles are abandoned. Therefore, it should be understood that these two views are termed "non-seeing" (*adarśana*).
The intent of that treatise is to state that by citing the nature of the category of "arising," it is explained that this is not itself a view;

thus, readers should understand how it corresponds to this passage. The third section of the treatise concludes with the meaning of the preparatory means (*upāya*), stating: first, by means of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one investigates that the essence of the view of self is fundamentally empty; by not giving rise to the conceptualization of various views, one finally attains entry into the corresponding samādhi. Therefore, it says: "This very observation serves as the means for entry."

Next, the third section below is the Buddha’s endorsement, which also serves as an exhortation for those practicing the Bodhisattva vehicle: just as previously stated regarding the view of a self being non-view, one should likewise know, see, and resolve with faith that all phenomena are both phenomena and non-phenomena.
Within this, first is the exposition and establishment, followed by the refutation of clinging to names.

Regarding "the bodhisattva who has resolved upon the mind," both the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom), and this treatise alike refer to the person who is a bodhisattva in practice.

Therefore, the treatise states: "Regarding those who have set out in the Bodhisattva Vehicle—this demonstrates which persons do not engage in conceptual discrimination. This answers the second preceding question.
It continues: "Those who practice the Bodhisattva Vehicle should be thus without conceptual discrimination."

Regarding the phrase "in all phenomena," this demonstrates which phenomena are not conceptually differentiated; it states that one does not differentiate with respect to all phenomena, and not merely with respect to the view of a self and so forth.

"One should know, see, and resolve with faith in this way" is the answer to the fourth question regarding the "expedient means. Now, according to the commentary’s explanation, once one has ceased such conceptual differentiation as previously described, it further states that "this very observation constitutes the expedient means for entry. Therefore, we know that the term "expedient means" encompasses all three preceding meanings.

Regarding "knowledge, vision, and resolute faith," there are three categories in the Sūtras, but the Śāstra classifies them as two, namely the training in concentration (*samādhi*) and the training in wisdom (*prajñā*), which correspond to the mind and cognition. During the two periods of cultivation, untainted (*anāsrava*) morality that accompanies them also constitutes the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*); however, because there is no separate stage for its cultivation, it is omitted here.
If that is so, how are the three phrases—knowledge (*jñāna*), vision (*darśana*), and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)—established?

The treatise states: "Knowledge, vision, and resolute conviction within non-conceptualization. This means that when cultivating non-conceptuality, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are cultivated separately as two; when cultivated together to enter meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), they become one. Thus, there are three phrases.

The initial statement, "one should know thus," teaches that at the time of practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one should know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-phenomena (*adharma*). The treatise states that if it is wisdom (*jñāna*), it is the non-conceptual wisdom of a person who practices;
relying upon *śamatha* (calm abiding) at the time of practicing concentration is termed the category of cessation (*śamatha-varga*).

Regarding those who cultivate non-conceptualization: if they cultivate various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and, based on these concentrations, give rise to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and other faculties to contemplate phenomena across time, one should know that both the concentrated mind and its objects, as well as the phenomena known therein, are all not the Dharma. This is because, as previously stated, the view of a self is not a true vision; therefore, it is said that one should understand things in this way.

Regarding "one should view it in this way," the *Śāstra* states: "Relying on vipaśyanā," which observes both principle and phenomena. This means that when a bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas with wisdom, they should also clearly perceive that dharmas are non-dharmas, just as the aforementioned view of self was not a [true] view. It is for this reason that it says, "one should view it in this way."
Because one observes phenomena with clarity through wisdom (*prajñā*), this is termed "view" (*darśana*), as it differs from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).

These two [concentration and wisdom] exist within the stage of application (*prayoga*); while concentration and wisdom increase accordingly, the cultivation of the two is not yet balanced. Therefore, regarding those who should thus have faith and understanding, they maintain both the mind of concentration and the mind of wisdom, resolving [the truth] at the moment of correctly entering true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*).

The Treatise states: "Because these two rely upon samādhi, they are 'resolute conviction' (adhimukti). At that time, one correctly discerns what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; because this is the understanding at the stage of verified faith, the Sūtra is titled "Faith and Understanding" (Śraddhādhimukta).
Because it is a superior understanding that surpasses prior cognition and vision, it is called "resolute belief" (adhimukti).
Thus, Asvabhāva’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states: "It refers to the arising of resolute belief through internal realization in correspondence with the dharmadhātu."
What is resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)?

The treatise states: "Because of mastery over *samādhi*. This refers to the stage of entering true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*), where one is free from the transformation of grasping at signs; thus it is called "mastery.
Because it surpasses the prior understanding that grasps signs, it is called "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*).

Furthermore, it says: "Understanding the images that are internal objects of focus is called 'resolute conviction' (adhimokṣa). This refers to the time of entering conventional observation; because one understands that internal phenomena within consciousness are like images and so forth, it is termed resolute conviction.

The treatise cites the sūtra’s conclusion, stating: "Having understood and comprehended in this way, one does not dwell on the notion of dharmas. Upon examining all extant versions of the text, this concluding passage is absent from all; it appears only here in the treatise’s citation of the sūtra. This single phrase concludes the preceding three phrases and summarizes the preceding three meanings.
Inferring from the flow of the text, even if [the term "non-dwelling"] is not explicitly present, it does not hinder the meaning.

As for the phrase "yet not dwelling on the notion of dharmas," this clarifies that when one attains this resolute conviction (adhimukti), there is no thought of attachment or dwelling toward any dharma; it is like having the notion of non-viewing while abiding in the view of a self. Therefore, the *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* states: "Just as one does not dwell on the marks of dharmas."
In Kumārajīva’s version, the phrase "not giving rise to the notion of dharmas" means not engendering attachment; however, it lacks the character *ru* (如).
This "non-abiding in notions" precisely reveals non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), whereas the preceding two—knowledge and vision—are preparatory applications (*prayoga*).

Alternatively, knowledge (*jñāna*), vision (*darśana*), and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)—these three types are all subsumed under the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). Since they do not yet abide in the true dharma, they constitute the two wisdoms of the fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) stages. Therefore, the treatise quotes the sūtra and concludes its explanation by stating: "Having thus known and understood, one does not dwell on the notion of dharmas. This precisely demonstrates non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).

The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Commentary on the Treatise) explains the three phrases as follows: "Through the two types of knowledge and samādhi, one thus attains detachment. This means that both mundane and supramundane knowledge—as described in the treatise in terms of knowing and seeing—rely upon samādhi; therefore, they are termed "resolute confidence" (*adhimokṣa*).
Because they can suppress and sever views of a self and of phenomena, they are termed "detachment" (*viveka*).

Next follows the second refutation of the attachment to names: the Buddha taught that one should not dwell on the notion of dharmas because there must be a notion of dharmas upon which to dwell; subsequently, he established the notion of dharmas as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The refutation of speech is precisely the perception of non-Dharma; this perception of non-Dharma is the meaning of "unshared" (asādhāraṇa).
This is called the perception of Dharma, which is the meaning of "associated" (saṃprayukta); all [terms] are to be explained according to the preceding interpretation.

From here begins the third major section of the treatise, titled "The Purity of Abiding in Untainted Conduct. Within this untainted state, there are two parts: first, the prose section clarifies that the Buddha remains untainted while preaching the Dharma; second, the verse section clarifies that the Buddha remains untainted within the cycle of saṃsāra.

This section consists of two parts: first, comparing great generosity and its abundant merit with the merit of teaching the Dharma without defilement, which is shown to be superior; this is intended to lead those who preach the Dharma to emulate the Buddha by teaching with a mind free from defilement.
Second, from the passage beginning "How does one teach for others," there is a question-and-answer explanation of the characteristics of teaching the Dharma without defilement.

Within the preceding section there are two parts: first, the presentation of great giving and its abundant merit; second, from the words "Good son" onwards, a comparison using that abundant merit to demonstrate that it is not equal to preaching the Dharma with a mind free from defilement.
The treatise consists of two parts: first, the designation of the title and its affiliation with the sutra; second, the formal explanation of the textual meaning.
Accordingly, the preceding analysis of the sutra is also divided into two sections, the significance of which is clear and easy to understand.

In the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Buddha himself explains this through two meanings: first, material giving is exhaustible while the giving of Dharma is inexhaustible. This reveals that because the material objects given during the act of giving are limited, such giving must eventually come to an end; whereas because the Dharma is limitless, its teaching never comes to an end.

Second, giving material wealth yields only worldly retributions; these were already obtained in the past and have already been lost, and though they may be obtained again now, they will inevitably be lost once more.

If, however, one preaches the Dharma with a mind free from defilement, one who has not yet attained certainty shall surely realize Great Nirvana; having attained it, one does not lose it, benefiting both oneself and others forever without end. This clarifies the difference in the timing of attaining the fruit.
The *Mahā-śāstra* states: Material giving yields finite fruits, yielding fruits bound to the desire realm, and yielding fruits bound to all three realms;
the giving of Dharma yields infinite fruits, yielding fruits both bound to and unbound from the three realms.

Those passages all refer to material giving with signs (*sanimitta*) in contrast to the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*); however, in this present section on the "Purity of Vision and Wisdom" (*darśana-jñāna-viśuddhi*), all the merits mentioned are signless giving (*animitta-dāna*), and their fruits are likewise immeasurable. Nevertheless, compared to the gift of Dharma, the gift of Dharma still excels in its merit. Wisdom is called the guide; it is precisely the Path-Dharma (*mārga-dharma*). Because merit serves as an aid, it brings about such great benefit; therefore, the Buddha exhorts its cultivation.
The Treatise says: "Because there is such great benefit, one must certainly expound it; yet while expounding it in this way, one remains undefiled.
Receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting are the causes for expounding the Dharma; therefore, these are mentioned together.

The *Śāstraviniścaya* by Vasubandhu states: "The emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) manifests merit; it is not that there is no inexhaustible merit. Although this refers to the activities performed by the Buddha’s emanation body, when he preaches the Dharma, there is inexhaustible merit; thus, he exhorts all students to teach with a mind free from defilement.
In the explanation through questions and answers, there are two points. The first question is:
"How is it that preaching the Dharma for others produces more merit than the great acts of giving mentioned previously?
The second question is: [as follows].
"How does one expound for others yet not be called 'expounding'?
The Buddha himself explains: "Not expounding" is what is called "expounding.
The Wei edition reads "not called expounding," while both the New Edition and others read "like" (ru), meaning that although one expounds, it is as if one were not expounding.

There are two meanings: first, one contemplates that the essence of both the speaker and the spoken is empty; thus, although one constantly expounds, it is as if one were not expounding at all. Therefore, the treatise states: "Because it is ineffable, it is not expounded. If those dharmas possessed an expressible essence, they should be expounded accordingly; otherwise, it would be defiled exposition because of its perversity. This means that if one does not contemplate the emptiness of the essence of speech, one speaks with a mind that grasps at signs, which is not undefiled exposition.

Kumārajīva said: "Not grasping at marks, one is like suchness, unmoving. This means that when preaching the Dharma, one is as if realizing true suchness (tathatā), free from all agitation; this corresponds to the other original statement, "As suchness does not expound."

Second, it is said that if one speaks with a mind attached to fame and profit, then even though one speaks constantly, it is as if one has not preached at all. Thus, the Treatise states: "Furthermore, when speaking in this manner, not coveting respect, offerings, and the like, is also 'speaking the Dharma without defilement. However, the Buddha’s teaching of "speaking the Dharma without defilement" at the conclusion of this sutra does not merely manifest that the Buddha himself is undefiled in his preaching; rather, the Buddha also instructs later generations to preach with an undefiled mind.

The *Śāstraviniścaya* by Vasubandhu states: "When the Buddhas teach the Dharma, they do not say, 'I am an emanation body' (nirmāṇakāya); because they do not speak in such a manner, their teaching is correct. The intent of that treatise is that when the Buddha teaches the Dharma, he does not say, "I am an emanation body," and thus he does not explicitly describe himself as such; this is the specific meaning [of the passage].

From here below is the second section, clarifying that the Buddha is unstained within the phenomena of saṃsāra and does not abide in birth and death; this treatise also refers to him as "one who does not abide in saṃsāra."

Previously, it was stated in general that the Buddha does not abide in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) because he has realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); here, nine specific modes of contemplative practice are explained to demonstrate his non-attachment amidst the process of transmigration, which serves to establish the aforementioned meaning of his non-abiding in birth-and-death.

Furthermore, although it was previously stated that the Buddha does not perceive any birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) in which he might abide, how could this preclude the existence of birth-and-death? This is because these nine kinds of birth-and-death phenomena observed by the Buddha are all illusory, like stars or visual distortions.
Although the Buddha dwells within birth and death, birth and death cannot defile him; this is called "flowing through saṃsāra without being stained.
Vasubandhu’s commentary on the following main text explains the sixth doubt, which asks:
"If all Buddhas and Tathāgatas constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, why is it said that the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa?"

This doubt arises regarding whether the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) has coming and going while the dharma-body (dharmakāya) is without coming and going; or else, it arises from the preceding point concerning why [the Buddha] does not preach the Dharma.
If one interprets it in this way, it is simply an elaboration from within the fifth section, and there is no separate sixth section.

To sever this doubt, nine contemplations are taught, as the verse states: "The nirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas is neither existent nor non-existent; because of the correct contemplation of the nine kinds of conditioned phenomena by means of sublime wisdom. This reveals that because the Buddhas have attained nirvāṇa, they do not abide in saṃsāra; yet because they manifest worldly conduct for the benefit of others, they do not abide in nirvāṇa. Thus, while they enter nirvāṇa through transformation, their Dharma-body remains eternally present.

The first two lines directly answer the doubt raised; the latter two lines clarify that while the nirmāṇakāya manifests worldly conduct, it does not abide within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), because it contemplates the conditioned through the nine contemplations.

This verse of the sutra is divided into three parts: first, a single line that generally identifies conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as the object of contemplation; second, two lines that properly employ nine metaphors to teach the contemplation of the nine [aspects] as the explanation of the conditioned; and finally, one line that concludes by exhorting practice.

The *Nengduan* (The Capable of Severing) states: "That which is produced by the conjunction of various factors" refers to the fact that the four marks and other such causes and conditions conjoin to cause what is produced to abide; thus it is called "produced.

Although the substance of uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) also undergoes transition and change, the followers of the Two Vehicles loathe and turn away from them; therefore, they are taught not to be defiled by them.
Alternatively, because they are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and produced by afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).

They cause sentient beings to sink into the defilements of birth and death; therefore, one teaches them not to be stained by these, by means of the nine contemplations (*navavipaśyanā*). The remainder is as explained by the Great Master in the previous fascicle.
